calculators.name: Body Mass Index (BMI) — WHO, WHO-Asian, CDC
calculators.whyRelevant: The universal entry-point anthropometric calculator; highest SEO volume in the category; pairs naturally with the Niro CWS wellness-score lead magnet (weight domain).

inputs.label: Classification standard
inputs.notes: Could also auto-branch via existing condition DSL context (ethnicity).

inputs.label: Age (adult gate)
inputs.notes: CDC adult categories apply to adults 20+ regardless of age/sex/race; children need BMI-for-age percentiles (separate tool, NOT expressible without LMS lookup data).

calculators.logic: FORMULA (WHO fact sheet, verbatim): BMI = 'weight (kg)/height² (m²)'. English-unit form (MedlinePlus): BMI = (weight in pounds × 703) ÷ (height in inches)². BANDS — WHO/CDC/NHLBI (verbatim from NHLBI Table IV-2 and CDC): Underweight <18.5; Normal 18.5–24.9 (CDC phrasing: '18.5 up to 25.0' = healthy weight); Overweight 25.0–29.9 (WHO: overweight = 'BMI greater than or equal to 25'); Obesity ≥30 (WHO: 'BMI greater than or equal to 30'); Obesity Class I 30.0–34.9; Class II 35.0–39.9; Class III ≥40 (NHLBI labels Class III 'Extreme'; CDC labels class 3 'severe', defined as 'BMI of 40 or higher', class 1 '30 to < 35', class 2 '35 to < 40'). WHO ASIAN ACTION POINTS (WHO Expert Consultation, Lancet 2004): public health action points at 23.0, 27.5, 32.5 and 37.5 kg/m²; BMI 23.0–27.4 = increased risk, ≥27.5 = high risk (commonly operationalized as overweight 23–27.5, obesity ≥27.5); WHO explicitly RETAINED the international classification — the Asian values are additional action points, not a replacement classification.
calculators.outputScale: BMI in kg/m², typically 10–60; category label

resultCategories.label: Underweight
resultCategories.interpretation: Below the healthy range; can be associated with undernutrition or illness.
resultCategories.recommendation: Discuss unintentional weight loss or persistently low weight with a healthcare professional.

resultCategories.label: Healthy weight
resultCategories.interpretation: Associated with the lowest weight-related disease risk for most adults.
resultCategories.recommendation: Maintain weight through balanced eating and regular physical activity.

resultCategories.label: Overweight
resultCategories.interpretation: NHLBI: disease risk (type 2 diabetes, hypertension, CVD) 'Increased', rising to 'High' when waist circumference is also elevated.
resultCategories.recommendation: Even modest weight loss reduces risk; combine dietary changes with increased activity, and check waist circumference for a fuller risk picture.

resultCategories.label: Obesity Class I
resultCategories.interpretation: NHLBI disease risk 'High' ('Very High' with elevated waist).
resultCategories.recommendation: Seek professional guidance; guideline-supported deficits of 500–750 kcal/day typically produce 1–2 lb (0.5–1 kg)/week loss (ACC/AHA/TOS via StatPearls).

resultCategories.label: Obesity Class II
resultCategories.interpretation: NHLBI disease risk 'Very High'.
resultCategories.recommendation: Medical evaluation recommended; discuss structured weight-management options with a clinician.

resultCategories.label: Obesity Class III (severe/extreme)
resultCategories.interpretation: NHLBI disease risk 'Extremely High'.
resultCategories.recommendation: See a healthcare professional to discuss comprehensive treatment options.

calculators.platformMapping: Fully expressible: derived parameter BMI = w/((h/100)*(h/100)) with unit conversion factors; category bands (min-inclusive edges: 18.5, 25.0, 30.0, 35.0, 40.0; Asian branch 23.0, 27.5, 32.5, 37.5 via condition DSL select/ethnicity context); direction lower-is-better above healthy band. English formula unnecessary if conversions normalize to kg/cm. NO missing primitives. (Child BMI percentile is NOT expressible — would need CDC LMS growth-chart lookup dataset.)
calculators.realWorldPresence: CDC Adult BMI Calculator, NHS healthy-weight (BMI) calculator, Mayo Clinic BMI calculator, Cleveland Clinic BMI article/tool, MDCalc BMI & BSA calculator.
calculators.cautions: Adults 20+ only; not for pregnancy; WHO calls BMI 'a surrogate marker of fatness' — can misclassify muscular people; recommend pairing with waist circumference (WHO fact sheet says waist 'can help the diagnosis of obesity'). Present WHO-Asian values as public-health action points, labeled by organization, alongside — never instead of — the retained international classification.

calculators.name: Body Surface Area (Mosteller & Du Bois)
calculators.whyRelevant: Common clinical utility (drug/chemo dosing, cardiac index); modest consumer search volume; cheap to build since inputs are shared with BMI.
calculators.logic: StatPearls (NBK559005), verbatim: Mosteller: 'BSA = √(height in cm) x (weight in kg) / 3600' i.e. BSA(m²) = sqrt(height_cm × weight_kg / 3600). Du Bois and Du Bois: 'BSA = 0.007184 x (height in cm)^0.725 x (weight in kg)^0.425'. Haycock (optional third): 'BSA = 0.024265 x (height in cm)^0.3964 x (weight in kg)^0.5378'. Primary refs: Mosteller RD, 'Simplified calculation of body-surface area', N Engl J Med 1987;317(17):1098; Du Bois D & Du Bois EF 1916 (Arch Intern Med).
calculators.outputScale: m², typically 1.0–2.5 for adults

resultCategories.label: Informational result
resultCategories.range: continuous m² value, no risk bands
resultCategories.interpretation: BSA estimates total skin surface area; used clinically for drug dosing and cardiac index, not as a health-risk score.
resultCategories.recommendation: For medication dosing decisions, rely on your clinician/pharmacist — formula choice can change the value by several percent.

No engine primitive is missing, and no result bands are needed for the informational output. Source, applicability, unit, content, and independent-review gates remain before authoring or publication.
calculators.realWorldPresence: MDCalc BSA calculator (Mosteller default, Du Bois shown), widely present in oncology/clinical references (StatPearls/NCBI).
calculators.cautions: Consumer-appropriate as an informational tool, but any dosing use is clinician-only — add a clear disclaimer. Report which formula produced the number.

calculators.name: Waist Circumference Risk (NIH / WHO / Asian cutoffs)
calculators.whyRelevant: Directly recommended by WHO and NHLBI as the companion to BMI; simple single-input tool; strong lead-magnet fit with wellness reports.

inputs.label: Waist circumference (midpoint between lowest rib and iliac crest, after normal exhale)

calculators.logic: NIH/NHLBI (verbatim): risk elevated when waist is 'more than 40 inches' (men) / 'more than 35 inches' (women); guideline table equivalents >102 cm men, >88 cm women. WHO 2008 (verbatim via PMC9224732): 'normal risk: ≤80 cm in females and ≤94 cm in males; increased risk: >80 cm in females and >94 cm in males; greatly increased risk: >88 cm in females and >102 cm in males'. Asian (IDF ethnic-specific, recorded in Alberti 2009 harmonizing statement): ≥90 cm men, ≥80 cm women define central obesity. CONFLICTS: kept per-organization; do not merge tiers.
calculators.outputScale: category label per selected standard (2–3 tiers)

resultCategories.label: Not elevated
resultCategories.range: NIH: ≤40 in (102 cm) men / ≤35 in (88 cm) women; WHO: ≤94 cm men / ≤80 cm women; Asian-IDF: <90 cm men / <80 cm women
resultCategories.interpretation: Abdominal-fat-related risk not elevated at this waist size.
resultCategories.recommendation: Maintain current habits; re-measure periodically using the same technique.

resultCategories.label: Increased risk (WHO tier 1)
resultCategories.range: WHO: >94 cm men / >80 cm women (up to 102/88)
resultCategories.interpretation: WHO associates this range with increased risk of metabolic complications.
resultCategories.recommendation: Consider modest weight reduction and more physical activity; discuss cardiometabolic screening (glucose, lipids, blood pressure) with a clinician.

resultCategories.label: Substantially increased / high risk
resultCategories.range: NIH & WHO: >102 cm (>40 in) men, >88 cm (>35 in) women; Asian-IDF central obesity from ≥90 cm men / ≥80 cm women
resultCategories.interpretation: NHLBI: at a given BMI, this waist size moves disease risk for type 2 diabetes, hypertension and CVD up a tier (e.g. 'Increased'→'High' in overweight; 'High'→'Very High' in Class I obesity); elevated waist can mark increased risk 'even in persons of normal weight'.
resultCategories.recommendation: Seek professional advice on weight management and cardiometabolic risk assessment; even without BMI change, reducing waist size lowers risk.

No missing primitives.
calculators.realWorldPresence: NHLBI patient education, CDC healthy-weight materials, NHS 'why waist size matters', Mayo Clinic obesity diagnosis pages.
calculators.cautions: Measurement technique matters (WHO midpoint protocol vs 'just above hipbones' consumer instruction — pick one, state it); not validated in pregnancy; cutoffs are population screening values, not diagnoses.

calculators.name: Waist-to-Hip Ratio (WHO 2008)
calculators.whyRelevant: Classic central-obesity index with WHO backing; moderate search volume; two inputs already collected for the Navy body-fat tool.
calculators.logic: FORMULA: WHR = waist_cm / hip_cm (unitless; same units both). CUTOFFS (WHO 2008 expert consultation, quoted via PMC9224732): abdominal obesity / substantially increased risk of metabolic complications at WHR 'above 0.90 for males and above 0.85 for females' (report tabulates as ≥0.90 men, ≥0.85 women).
calculators.outputScale: ratio ~0.6–1.2; two-tier category by sex

resultCategories.label: Lower risk
resultCategories.interpretation: Fat distribution pattern not indicating abdominal obesity by WHO criteria.
resultCategories.recommendation: Maintain healthy habits; ratio is best tracked with consistent measurement technique.

resultCategories.label: Abdominal obesity — substantially increased risk
resultCategories.interpretation: WHO associates this ratio with substantially increased risk of metabolic complications.
resultCategories.recommendation: Discuss cardiometabolic risk screening with a clinician; weight management focused on abdominal fat (activity + dietary change) is advised.

sources.title: Waist circumference and waist-hip ratio: report of a WHO expert consultation (8-11 Dec 2008)

calculators.platformMapping: Fully expressible: derived ratio (waist/hip), sex-branched bands via condition DSL, unit conversions. Edge control: WHO uses ≥ (min-inclusive). No missing primitives.
calculators.realWorldPresence: Referenced across NIH/PMC literature and WHO documents; common on hospital-system patient pages; less prominent than waist alone in current NHS/NICE messaging (NICE prefers waist-to-height).
calculators.cautions: WHO 2008 report PDF itself was 403-blocked to automated fetch — cutoffs verified via peer-reviewed secondary; note hip measurement adds error vs waist-only indices; not for pregnancy.

calculators.name: Waist-to-Height Ratio (NICE)
calculators.whyRelevant: The newest guideline-endorsed consumer metric ('keep your waist to less than half your height') — very memorable message, strong content/SEO angle, one extra input beyond BMI.

inputs.label: BMI (optional gate)
inputs.notes: NICE positions WHtR for adults with BMI below 35 kg/m², used alongside BMI; if BMI ≥35, suppress WHtR interpretation.

calculators.logic: FORMULA: WHtR = waist / height (same units, unitless). NICE classification (NG246, 'Overweight and obesity management', published 14 January 2025, carrying forward the 2022 CG189 update; values via NICE-domain search snippets because nice.org.uk blocks automated fetch): 'healthy central adiposity: waist-to-height ratio of 0.4 to 0.49, indicating no increased health risks; increased central adiposity: 0.5 to 0.59; high central adiposity: 0.6 or more, indicating further increased health risk'. Applies to adults with BMI below 35 kg/m², used alongside BMI as a practical estimate of central adiposity to predict risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension and cardiovascular disease. Public message: keep your waist to less than half your height (ratio under 0.5). Evidence note: cut-off ~0.5 held 'for all ethnicities and sexes'.
calculators.outputScale: ratio ~0.3–0.8; three categories

resultCategories.label: Healthy central adiposity
resultCategories.interpretation: No increased health risk from central fat per NICE.
resultCategories.recommendation: Keep your waist to less than half your height; maintain current activity and diet.

resultCategories.label: Increased central adiposity
resultCategories.interpretation: Increased risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension and cardiovascular disease.
resultCategories.recommendation: NICE's consumer message: aim to keep waist below half of height; consider lifestyle change and a health-professional review of cardiometabolic risk.

resultCategories.label: High central adiposity
resultCategories.interpretation: Further increased health risk per NICE.
resultCategories.recommendation: Seek advice from a healthcare professional about weight management and risk screening.

calculators.platformMapping: Fully expressible: derived ratio; three category bands (0.4/0.5/0.6 min-inclusive edges); optional condition-DSL gate on derived BMI <35; unit conversions. Sub-0.4 handling: NICE bands start at 0.4 — show 'below defined healthy band' informational state rather than inventing a category. No missing primitives.
calculators.realWorldPresence: NHS digital 'height and weight/waist' tools incorporate the message; NICE NG246 is the anchor guideline; widely covered by UK health services.
calculators.cautions: nice.org.uk 403-blocks automated fetch — bands are search-verified from NICE's own domain and a PMC editorial; confirm verbatim text manually before launch. Do not interpret for BMI ≥35, children (separate NICE advice), or pregnancy.

calculators.name: Body Fat % — US Navy Circumference Method (+ ACE categories)
calculators.whyRelevant: Most-searched tape-measure body-fat method; self-service inputs only; pairs with ACE category table for interpretation — classic lead-magnet calculator.

inputs.label: Men: abdomen at navel / Women: natural waist (narrowest torso point)
Hip circumference (women only, widest point)
inputs.notes: Required when sex=female (conditional requirement).

calculators.logic: EQUATIONS (verbatim from PMC10282178, Hodgdon & Beckett 1984 / Hodgdon & Friedl 1999; inputs in cm are divided by 2.54, i.e. equations operate in inches): MEN: '% body fat = 86.010 x log10((abdomen − neck)/2.54) − 70.041 x log10(height/2.54) + 36.76'. WOMEN: '% body fat = 163.205 x log10((waist + hip − neck)/2.54) − 97.684 x log10(height/2.54) − 78.387'. Reported standard error of estimate 3%–4% BF. ALTERNATE density form (Hodgdon-Beckett 1984, cm units; NOT verified from an allowed source — record but flag): men body density = 1.0324 − 0.19077×log10(waist−neck) + 0.15456×log10(height); women 1.29579 − 0.35004×log10(waist+hip−neck) + 0.22100×log10(height); %BF = 495/density − 450 (Siri). INTERPRETATION TABLE (ACE — American Council on Exercise body-fat norms; reproduced widely, ACE site not in allowed domain list): Essential fat: women 10–13%, men 2–5%; Athletes: women 14–20%, men 6–13%; Fitness: women 21–24%, men 14–17%; Acceptable/Average: women 25–31%, men 18–24%; Obesity: women 32%+, men 25%+.
calculators.outputScale: % body fat, roughly 2–60%; ACE category label

resultCategories.label: Essential fat
resultCategories.interpretation: Minimum fat needed for basic physiological function; women's higher essential fat supports hormonal/reproductive function.
resultCategories.recommendation: Values this low are not a goal for the general public; sustained levels near essential fat warrant professional supervision.

resultCategories.label: Athletes
resultCategories.interpretation: Typical of athletic body composition.
resultCategories.recommendation: Maintain only with adequate nutrition and training support.

resultCategories.label: Fitness
resultCategories.interpretation: Lean, fit range.
resultCategories.recommendation: Maintain regular activity and balanced diet.

resultCategories.label: Acceptable
resultCategories.interpretation: Common, generally acceptable range for adults.
resultCategories.recommendation: Focus on activity and diet quality rather than the number alone.

resultCategories.label: Obesity
resultCategories.interpretation: Excess body fat associated with elevated health risk.
resultCategories.recommendation: Consider discussing weight management with a healthcare professional; combine with waist and BMI measures for context.

calculators.name: Ideal Body Weight (Devine, + Robinson/Miller/Hamwi)
calculators.whyRelevant: High search volume ('ideal weight for my height'); simple; but interpretation needs care because 'ideal' is a drug-dosing construct, not a health target.

inputs.label: Height
inputs.notes: Formulas defined per inch over 5 ft (60 in); many sources state they are 'only recommended if the patient's height is over 5 ft (152 cm)' (PMC10621523).

calculators.logic: Verbatim (PMC8646317 'Ideal body weight: a commentary'): DEVINE — men '50 kg + (2.3 kg per inch over 5′)'; women '45.5 kg + (2.3 kg per inch over 5′)'. ROBINSON et al 1983 — men '52 kg + (1.9 kg per inch over 5′)'; women '49 kg + (1.7 kg per inch over 5′)'. MILLER et al 1983 — men '55.7 kg + (1.39 kg per inch over 5′)'; women '53 kg + (1.33 kg per inch over 5′)'. HAMWI 1964 — men '106 lb + (6 lb per inch over 5′)'; women '100 lb + (5 lb per inch over 5′)'. Provenance: Devine BJ, 'Gentamicin therapy', Drug Intell Clin Pharm 1974;8:650-655 — originally for drug-dose estimation (per Pai & Paloucek, 'The origin of the ideal body weight equations', Ann Pharmacother 2000). ADJUSTED body weight for obesity (commonly ABW = IBW + 0.4×(actual − IBW)) exists on MDCalc's IBW/ABW calculator but the 0.4 factor was NOT verifiable from an allowed source this session — flag before shipping. Note: different IBW formulas disagree by up to 14–19% (PMC10621523).
calculators.outputScale: kg (or lb for Hamwi), typically 40–100 kg

resultCategories.label: Informational estimate
resultCategories.interpretation: A formula-based reference weight originally created for medication dosing — not a medically defined 'goal weight'; formulas disagree with each other by double-digit percentages.
resultCategories.recommendation: Use the healthy BMI-derived weight RANGE for goal-setting instead of a single IBW number; consult a clinician or dietitian for individual targets.

sources.title: Ideal body weight: a commentary (PMC8646317) — all four formulas verbatim
Variability in ideal body weight formulae (PMC10621523) — height >5 ft limitation, 14-19% inter-formula spread
Pai MP, Paloucek FP. The origin of the 'ideal' body weight equations. Ann Pharmacother 2000;34(9):1066-9 (PMID 10981254); Devine BJ, Drug Intell Clin Pharm 1974;8:650-655
Ideal Body Weight and Adjusted Body Weight calculator

calculators.platformMapping: Fully expressible: derived formula base + slope × max(0, height_in − 60) (max() is whitelisted); sex + formula branches via condition DSL/option select; Hamwi lb→kg via conversion factor 0.45359237. Floor rule: for height <60 in, show 'formula not defined below 5 ft' (engine floor/validation rule). No missing primitives.
calculators.realWorldPresence: MDCalc IBW/ABW (clinical staple); NIH/PMC literature; ubiquitous consumer 'ideal weight' calculators.
calculators.cautions: Do NOT present as a weight-loss target — frame as a dosing-heritage reference vs the healthy-BMI range; undefined below 5 ft; large inter-formula disagreement must be surfaced, not averaged.

calculators.name: Lean Body Mass (Boer)
calculators.whyRelevant: Popular among fitness users (protein targets, FFMI adjacent); shares inputs with BMR tools; clinically used for contrast/drug dosing in obesity.
calculators.logic: BOER 1984 (verbatim structure from PMC6110034): men LBM(kg) = 0.407·W + 0.267·H − 19.2; women LBM(kg) = 0.252·W + 0.473·H − 48.3, with W = weight in kg and H = height in CENTIMETERS (the PMC extraction labeled H '(m)' but the coefficients are only dimensionally consistent with cm — e.g. 70 kg/175 cm man: 0.407×70 + 0.267×175 − 19.2 = 56.0 kg; flagged in openIssues for confirmation against Boer 1984 primary). Citation: Boer P. 'Estimated lean body mass as an index for normalization of body fluid volumes in humans.' Am J Physiol 1984;247:F632-636. Comparator (same PMC source): James formula plateaus at BMI ~37 (women)/~43 (men); Boer considered preferable at BMI ≥35.
calculators.outputScale: kg lean mass; optionally show LBM% of weight

resultCategories.label: Informational estimate
resultCategories.interpretation: Formula estimate of fat-free mass; no consumer risk bands exist from allowed authorities.
resultCategories.recommendation: For body-composition tracking prefer consistent method over time; DXA/BIA measure rather than estimate — treat this as an approximation.

Boer P. Estimated lean body mass as an index for normalization of body fluid volumes in humans. Am J Physiol. 1984;247:F632-F636

calculators.platformMapping: Fully expressible: linear derived formulas with sex branch; unit conversions. No missing primitives. Optional derived body-fat-from-LBM: fatMass = weight − LBM; %fat = 100×(weight−LBM)/weight.
calculators.realWorldPresence: MDCalc Lean Body Weight calculator; radiology/anesthesia dosing literature (NIH/PMC); mainstream fitness calculators.
calculators.cautions: Population-average regression — not accurate for very muscular or sarcopenic individuals; adults only; confirm height-unit convention (cm) against the 1984 primary before launch (see openIssues).

calculators.name: Calorie / BMR / TDEE Calculator (Mifflin-St Jeor primary; revised Harris-Benedict alternate)
calculators.whyRelevant: The market packages BMR + activity multiplier + calorie needs as one tool (inventory: calorie-bmr-tdee); combined per dedup review D3 cluster 5. Mifflin-St Jeor is the primary method per the ADA evidence review; revised Harris-Benedict is the labeled alternate; TDEE = BMR x activity factor.
calculators.realWorldPresence: Offered as a single combined calculator on MDCalc, Mayo Clinic (calorie calculator), NIDDK-adjacent tools and Omni; see mergedFrom entries for each component’s original presence.

inputs.label: Age
inputs.notes: Derivation cohort was healthy adults ~19-78 y.

options.label: Extra active — very hard exercise + physical job (×1.9)

calculators.logic: Method select: Mifflin-St Jeor (primary) or revised Harris-Benedict (alternate) computes BMR/REE from weight, height, age, sex; TDEE = BMR x activity multiplier (1.2 sedentary .. 1.9 very active, StatPearls-anchored; intermediate values labeled convention). All verbatim coefficients, bands and caveats preserved unchanged in mergedFrom.
calculators.outputScale: kcal/day (BMR and TDEE)

resultCategories.label: Maintenance calories
resultCategories.interpretation: Estimated daily calories to maintain current weight at the selected activity level.
resultCategories.recommendation: Cross-check against the Dietary Guidelines ranges (women 1,600-2,400; men 2,000-3,000 kcal/day) — if your result falls far outside, re-check the activity level chosen.

resultCategories.label: Guideline-consistent weight-loss target
resultCategories.interpretation: Per ACC/AHA/TOS guidance (via StatPearls), this deficit typically yields ~1-2 lb (0.5-1 kg)/week loss.
resultCategories.recommendation: Do not go below general minimums without medical supervision; sustained very-low-calorie diets require clinical oversight.

mergedFrom.name: BMR / RMR — Mifflin-St Jeor
mergedFrom.whyRelevant: The most validated RMR equation for healthy adults (best performer in Frankenfield's ADA systematic review) and the default engine behind every 'calorie calculator' — core to a wellness lead magnet.

inputs.label: Age
inputs.notes: Derivation cohort was healthy adults ~19-78 y.

mergedFrom.logic: ORIGINAL PUBLISHED COEFFICIENTS (verbatim via PMC9967803, quoting Mifflin et al. Am J Clin Nutr 1990;51:241-247): Males REE(kcal/day) = (9.99 × wt kg) + (6.25 × ht cm) − (4.92 × age y) + 5; Females = (9.99 × wt kg) + (6.25 × ht cm) − (4.92 × age y) − 161. (Equivalent single-equation form in the primary: 9.99W + 6.25H − 4.92A + 166×sex[m=1,f=0] − 161.) WIDELY USED ROUNDED FORM (popularized in clinical practice; e.g. Frankenfield 2005 ADA review context): 10W + 6.25H − 5A + 5 (men) / − 161 (women) — the platform should implement the ORIGINAL coefficients and may display the rounded form as a note. Validation context: 'most reliable, predicting RMR within 10% of measured in more nonobese and obese individuals than any other equation' (Frankenfield systematic review, PMID 15883556).

resultCategories.label: Resting energy estimate
resultCategories.interpretation: Estimated calories burned at complete rest; individual true RMR commonly deviates ±10%.
resultCategories.recommendation: Use as the base for TDEE; for medical nutrition decisions (e.g. clinical weight management) consult a dietitian — indirect calorimetry is the measurement standard.

sources.title: Revised Harris-Benedict Equation: New Human Resting Metabolic Rate Equation (PMC9967803) — tabulates Mifflin coefficients verbatim
Mifflin MD, St Jeor ST, et al. A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure in healthy individuals. Am J Clin Nutr 1990;51:241-247
Frankenfield D et al. Comparison of predictive equations for resting metabolic rate in healthy nonobese and obese adults: a systematic review. J Am Diet Assoc 2005 (PMID 15883556)

mergedFrom.platformMapping: Fully expressible: linear derived formula, sex branch (constant +5 vs −161 via condition DSL or ternary), unit conversions, round() for display. No missing primitives.
mergedFrom.realWorldPresence: MDCalc Mifflin-St Jeor calculator; Mayo Clinic calorie calculator (Mifflin-based); NIH Body Weight Planner (related NIDDK model); virtually all consumer TDEE calculators.
mergedFrom.cautions: Healthy adults only (derivation 19–78 y); ±10% typical error, larger in obesity; not for pregnancy, children, or clinical illness; publish which coefficient set (original vs rounded) the engine runs.

mergedFrom.name: BMR — Revised Harris-Benedict (Roza & Shizgal 1984)
mergedFrom.whyRelevant: Second-most-searched BMR equation; offered as an alternative engine next to Mifflin (conflict surfaced, not merged).
mergedFrom.logic: REVISED Harris-Benedict, Roza & Shizgal 1984 (verbatim via PMC9967803): Males BMR(kcal/day) = (13.397 × wt kg) + (4.799 × ht cm) − (5.677 × age y) + 88.362; Females = (9.247 × wt kg) + (3.098 × ht cm) − (4.330 × age y) + 447.593. ORIGINAL Harris-Benedict 1918-1919 (same source, for reference/education): Males = (13.75 × W) + (5.003 × H) − (6.755 × A) + 66.47; Females = (9.563 × W) + (1.850 × H) − (4.676 × A) + 655.1. Citation: Roza AM, Shizgal HM. 'The Harris Benedict equation reevaluated: resting energy requirements and the body cell mass.' Am J Clin Nutr 1984;40:168-182. Known behavior vs Mifflin: Harris-Benedict tends to overestimate RMR (Frankenfield 2005) — surface as an inter-authority difference.

resultCategories.label: Resting energy estimate
resultCategories.interpretation: Alternative BMR estimate; typically reads slightly higher than Mifflin-St Jeor for the same person.
resultCategories.recommendation: Prefer Mifflin-St Jeor for accuracy per the ADA systematic review; when the two disagree, that spread is the honest uncertainty band.

sources.title: Revised Harris-Benedict Equation: New Human Resting Metabolic Rate Equation (PMC9967803)
Roza AM, Shizgal HM. Am J Clin Nutr 1984;40:168-182 (PMID 6741850)

mergedFrom.platformMapping: Fully expressible: linear derived formulas with sex branch; no missing primitives.
mergedFrom.realWorldPresence: Ubiquitous in consumer calorie calculators; clinical nutrition texts; MDCalc offers Harris-Benedict variants.
mergedFrom.cautions: Adults only; overestimation tendency vs measured RMR; keep original-1919 version clearly labeled as historical if displayed.

mergedFrom.name: TDEE — Activity Multipliers
mergedFrom.whyRelevant: The conversion layer that turns BMR into the number users actually want (daily calories); inseparable from the BMR calculators in search intent.

options.label: Extra active — very hard exercise + physical job (×1.9)

mergedFrom.logic: TDEE = BMR × activity factor. VERIFIED from an allowed source (StatPearls NBK576400, verbatim): 'Multiplying the calculated BMR by an activity factor reflecting the individual's level of physical activity (ranging from 1.2 for sedentary to 1.9 for very active) estimates the TDEE' (worked example uses 1.6 for moderate activity). The full conventional five-step ladder 1.2 / 1.375 / 1.55 / 1.725 / 1.9 with the labels above is an exercise-nutrition CONVENTION implemented by MDCalc and essentially all TDEE calculators; no single authoritative primary source for the exact intermediate values exists within the allowed domains (see openIssues) — the endpoints (1.2, 1.9) and the multiplication method are StatPearls-verified. Deficit guidance for downstream use (StatPearls quoting ACC/AHA/TOS): 'An energy deficit of 500 to 750 kcal per day usually results in a weight loss of approximately 1 to 2 lb (0.5 to 1 kg) per week.'

resultCategories.label: Maintenance calories
resultCategories.interpretation: Estimated daily calories to maintain current weight at the selected activity level.
resultCategories.recommendation: Cross-check against the Dietary Guidelines ranges (women 1,600-2,400; men 2,000-3,000 kcal/day) — if your result falls far outside, re-check the activity level chosen.

resultCategories.label: Guideline-consistent weight-loss target
resultCategories.interpretation: Per ACC/AHA/TOS guidance (via StatPearls), this deficit typically yields ~1-2 lb (0.5-1 kg)/week loss.
resultCategories.recommendation: Do not go below general minimums without medical supervision; sustained very-low-calorie diets require clinical oversight.

sources.title: Management of Weight Loss Plateau (NBK576400) — activity-factor method, 1.2-1.9 range, 500-750 kcal deficit
Mifflin-St Jeor Equation calculator (implements the 1.2/1.375/1.55/1.725/1.9 ladder)

mergedFrom.platformMapping: Fully expressible: option select → multiplier via optionPoints/lookup table (points→value), then derived multiplication with the BMR calculator's output; round() for display. No missing primitives.
mergedFrom.realWorldPresence: MDCalc, Mayo Clinic calorie calculator, and effectively every consumer TDEE/macro calculator use this ladder.
mergedFrom.cautions: Users systematically overestimate activity level (note this in UI copy); the intermediate multipliers are convention rather than guideline values — label them as commonly used estimates; not for children, pregnancy, or clinical nutrition planning.

calculators.name: Daily Calorie Needs Context (Dietary Guidelines for Americans)
calculators.whyRelevant: Authoritative US-government context layer for TDEE results; low build cost (lookup table); strengthens E-E-A-T of the calorie cluster.

options.label: Sedentary — only light physical activity of independent daily life
Moderately active — activity equivalent to walking about 1.5 to 3 miles per day at 3 to 4 mph, plus daily-life activity
Active — activity equivalent to walking more than 3 miles per day at 3 to 4 mph, plus daily-life activity

calculators.logic: Source: Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2020-2025, Appendix 2 'Estimated Calorie Needs per Day, by Age, Sex, and Physical Activity Level' (Table A2-1), derived from the IOM Estimated Energy Requirement (EER) equations using reference heights and weights. VERIFIED overall adult ranges: females 1,600-2,400 kcal/day; males 2,000-3,000 kcal/day (range spans age and activity level; within each age group, needs rise from sedentary to active, and fall with age). The 'moderately active' walking-equivalence definition (1.5-3 miles/day at 3-4 mph) is search-verified. The FULL per-age-band cell values could NOT be captured because dietaryguidelines.gov 403-blocks automated fetch — the complete Table A2-1 must be transcribed manually before this lookup ships (openIssues).
calculators.outputScale: kcal/day range (e.g. '1,800-2,200')

resultCategories.label: Adult female overall range
resultCategories.interpretation: US-government estimated maintenance range across adult ages and activity levels.
resultCategories.recommendation: Treat as population estimates for group planning; individual needs vary — pair with the personalized TDEE result.

resultCategories.label: Adult male overall range
resultCategories.interpretation: As above for men.
resultCategories.recommendation: As above; older and sedentary adults sit at the bottom of the range, young active adults at the top.

sources.title: Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020-2025 — Appendix 2, Table A2-1
2015-2020 Dietary Guidelines Appendix 2 (same table lineage)

calculators.platformMapping: Fully expressible once data is transcribed: pure lookup table keyed by sex × age-band × activity (existing lookup primitive); no formulas. The underlying IOM EER equations are NOT needed (table is precomputed), but if ever implemented directly they use only linear terms — expressible.
calculators.realWorldPresence: dietaryguidelines.gov, MyPlate.gov calorie plans, Mayo Clinic calorie calculator references DGA ranges.
calculators.cautions: Population reference values, not prescriptions; pregnancy/lactation have separate needs (out of scope); complete Table A2-1 transcription pending manual verification (403 block).

calculators.name: Blood Pressure Category (ACC/AHA)
calculators.whyRelevant: Highest-traffic vitals tool; BP appears on every wellness/lab report; direct companion to existing Heart Risk calculator and the Niro CWS blood-pressure biomarkers.

inputs.label: Systolic blood pressure (top number)
inputs.notes: Resting, seated reading. Consumer devices report mmHg universally; no unit conversion offered.

inputs.label: If reading is higher than 180/120: chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, change in vision or difficulty speaking?
inputs.notes: Only used to split Severe Hypertension vs Hypertensive Emergency messaging; hidden unless reading exceeds 180/120.

calculators.logic: AHA table verbatim (heart.org, last reviewed Aug 14, 2025): NORMAL = systolic LESS THAN 120 and diastolic LESS THAN 80. ELEVATED = systolic 120-129 and diastolic LESS THAN 80. STAGE 1 HYPERTENSION = systolic 130-139 or diastolic 80-89. STAGE 2 HYPERTENSION = systolic 140 OR HIGHER or diastolic 90 OR HIGHER. SEVERE HYPERTENSION = HIGHER THAN 180 and/or HIGHER THAN 120 without symptoms (call your health care professional). HYPERTENSIVE EMERGENCY = HIGHER THAN 180 and/or HIGHER THAN 120 with symptoms (call 911). Aggregation rule implied by the and/or column: final category = the WORSE of the systolic-implied and diastolic-implied categories; ELEVATED additionally requires diastolic <80. Note edge semantics: crisis threshold is strictly greater than 180 / greater than 120 (a reading of exactly 180/120 is Stage 2).

resultCategories.label: Normal
resultCategories.interpretation: Blood pressure is in the normal range.
resultCategories.recommendation: Stick with heart-healthy habits such as a balanced diet and regular exercise (AHA).

resultCategories.label: Elevated
resultCategories.interpretation: Blood pressure is elevated; risk of progressing to hypertension.
resultCategories.recommendation: Adopt or maintain heart-healthy habits; the goal is to prevent reaching Stage 1 hypertension (AHA).

resultCategories.label: Stage 1 Hypertension
resultCategories.interpretation: High blood pressure, Stage 1. Only a health professional can confirm a hypertension diagnosis.
resultCategories.recommendation: AHA: your health care professional should prescribe lifestyle changes and may consider medication based on your risk of heart disease or stroke, and should add medication if you have diabetes, heart failure or kidney disease.

resultCategories.label: Stage 2 Hypertension
resultCategories.interpretation: High blood pressure, Stage 2.
resultCategories.recommendation: AHA: your health care professional should prescribe blood pressure medication and lifestyle changes.

resultCategories.label: Severe Hypertension (no symptoms)
resultCategories.interpretation: Severely elevated reading.
resultCategories.recommendation: AHA: wait 1 minute and take your blood pressure again. If still this high and you have no symptoms, contact your health care professional; they may start or adjust medication.

resultCategories.label: Hypertensive Emergency
resultCategories.range: SBP >180 AND/OR DBP >120 WITH symptoms (chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, change in vision, difficulty speaking)
resultCategories.interpretation: Medical emergency.
resultCategories.recommendation: Call 911 immediately (AHA).

sources.title: Understanding Blood Pressure Readings (Last Reviewed: Aug 14, 2025)

Whelton PK et al. 2017 ACC/AHA/AAPA/ABC/ACPM/AGS/APhA/ASH/ASPC/NMA/PCNA Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (categories originate here)

calculators.platformMapping: Existing primitives only. Numeric band scoring on systolic (ordinal points: <120 -> 0 [max-exclusive 120]; 120-129 -> 1; 130-139 -> 2; 140-180 -> 3 [max-inclusive 180]; >180 -> 4 [min-exclusive 180]) and on diastolic (<80 -> 0; 80-89 -> 2; 90-120 -> 3 [max-inclusive 120]; >120 -> 4). max() aggregation of the two ordinal scores; lookup table points->category label; direction lower-is-better. The Elevated definition (requires DBP <80) falls out naturally from max(1, 0)=1 vs max(1, >=2). Optional crisisSymptoms select via option points + condition DSL branches category 4 into two messages. Min-inclusive/exclusive edge control is required and exists.
calculators.realWorldPresence: heart.org own category checker; Mayo Clinic, Cleveland Clinic, NHS BP charts; every major health portal.
calculators.cautions: Diagnosis requires a clinician and repeated readings; single readings mis-classify. Must show 911 guidance for emergency band. Educational-use disclaimer required. Category table updated by AHA Aug 2025 (Severe Hypertension vs Hypertensive Emergency split) - keep synced with heart.org.

calculators.name: Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP)
calculators.whyRelevant: Simple derived vital; common lab-report/clinical adjunct to the BP tool; trivially expressible in the engine.

inputs.label: Mean arterial pressure (computed)
inputs.notes: map = diastolic + (systolic - diastolic)/3, equivalently (systolic + 2*diastolic)/3

calculators.logic: StatPearls (DeMers & Wachs, Physiology, Mean Arterial Pressure) verbatim: 'MAP = DP + 1/3(SP - DP) or MAP = DP + 1/3(PP)' where PP = pulse pressure. Perfusion floor verbatim: 'to perfuse vital organs requires the maintenance of a minimum MAP of 60 mmHg'; below it 'end-organ manifestations such as ischemia and infarction can occur.' No authoritative consumer normal range exists (StatPearls declines to give one). Research-context bands only (Kandil et al., Biomedicines 2023, PMC10046034, citing Kundu et al. 2017): Optimal <93.33; Normal 93.33-99.00; High normal 99.01-105.67; Grade 1 105.68-119.00; Grade 2 119.01-132.33; Grade 3 >=132.34 mmHg - label as research proposal, not guideline.

resultCategories.label: Below perfusion threshold
resultCategories.interpretation: Below the minimum MAP of 60 mmHg that StatPearls cites as required to perfuse vital organs.
resultCategories.recommendation: A reading this low from a home cuff most often reflects measurement error, but true low MAP is serious - re-measure and seek medical advice promptly, especially with dizziness or fainting.

resultCategories.label: At or above perfusion threshold
resultCategories.interpretation: At or above the minimum organ-perfusion threshold. MAP has no consumer 'normal range' endorsed by a major guideline; interpret blood pressure itself with the ACC/AHA categories.
resultCategories.recommendation: Use the blood pressure category tool for interpretation; discuss persistent abnormalities with a clinician.

sources.title: DeMers D, Wachs D. Physiology, Mean Arterial Pressure

Kandil H et al. Using Mean Arterial Pressure in Hypertension Diagnosis versus Using Either Systolic or Diastolic Blood Pressure Measurements. Biomedicines. 2023 (research MAP bands, citing Kundu et al. 2017)

calculators.platformMapping: Existing primitives only: derived parameter map = diastolic + (systolic - diastolic)/3 (uses + - /; round() available for display). Category bands on map with min-inclusive edge at 60. Optional research bands as a second band set behind a context flag (condition DSL).
calculators.realWorldPresence: MDCalc Mean Arterial Pressure calculator; ubiquitous in nursing/clinical references; common on consumer calculator sites.
calculators.cautions: The cuff-formula MAP is an estimate (true MAP requires invasive measurement). Do not present the research hypertension-by-MAP bands as guideline categories. Low-value alerts must be conservative (measurement error common).

calculators.name: Pulse Pressure
calculators.whyRelevant: Zero-extra-input companion to the BP tool; arterial-stiffness education angle; strong SEO pairing with MAP.

inputs.label: Pulse pressure (computed)
inputs.notes: pp = systolic - diastolic; also derive ppFraction = pp / systolic for the narrow-PP rule

calculators.logic: Formula (StatPearls NBK482408, Homan/Bordes/Cichowski, verbatim): 'Pulse Pressure = Systolic Blood Pressure - Diastolic Blood Pressure.' Normal approximately 40 mmHg (StatPearls; Mayo: 120/80 gives PP 40, 'considered a healthy pulse pressure'). Narrow (StatPearls): PP less than 25% of systolic pressure is 'inappropriately low or narrowed'. High thresholds CONFLICT - both surfaced: Mayo Clinic: 'Generally, a pulse pressure greater than 40 mm Hg is unhealthy' and 'A pulse pressure greater than 60 is a risk factor for heart disease, especially for older adults.' StatPearls: PP greater than 100 mmHg is 'high or widened', and 'as little as a 10 mmHg increase in the pulse pressure increases the cardiovascular risk by as much as 20%.'

resultCategories.label: Narrow pulse pressure
resultCategories.interpretation: Lower than expected relative to systolic pressure; can occur with blood loss, heart-pump problems, or measurement artifact.
resultCategories.recommendation: Re-measure; discuss a persistently narrow pulse pressure with a clinician.

resultCategories.label: Healthy / typical
resultCategories.interpretation: Around 40 mmHg is cited as a healthy pulse pressure (Mayo, StatPearls).
resultCategories.recommendation: Maintain heart-healthy habits: no smoking/vaping, healthy diet, regular exercise, healthy weight, stress management, 7-9 hours sleep, control BP/cholesterol/blood sugar (Mayo).

resultCategories.label: Above typical
resultCategories.interpretation: Mayo notes a pulse pressure greater than 40 mmHg is generally considered unhealthy; often reflects arterial stiffening.
resultCategories.recommendation: Focus on the lifestyle measures above and on blood pressure control; discuss with a clinician at routine care.

resultCategories.label: Elevated - risk factor
resultCategories.range: >60 mmHg (Mayo); StatPearls separately labels >100 mmHg 'high or widened'
resultCategories.interpretation: A pulse pressure greater than 60 is a risk factor for heart disease, especially in older adults; largely driven by stiffness of the large arteries (Mayo).
resultCategories.recommendation: Bring the reading to your care team; manage blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar. Note: BP medicines may not lower pulse pressure itself (Mayo).

sources.title: Pulse pressure: An indicator of heart health? (Aug 18, 2023)
Homan TD, Bordes SJ, Cichowski E. Physiology, Pulse Pressure (updated Jul 10, 2023)

calculators.platformMapping: Existing primitives only: derived pp = systolic - diastolic; derived narrowFlag = (pp / systolic) < 0.25 via ternary (pp/systolic < 0.25 ? 1 : 0). Category bands on pp with the narrow override implemented as condition DSL / max() on an override band. Conflict display (Mayo >60 vs StatPearls >100) uses the platform's dual-attribution pattern.
calculators.realWorldPresence: Mayo Clinic explainer; MDCalc-adjacent references; common on BP-tracker apps.
calculators.cautions: Mayo and StatPearls disagree on the 'high' threshold - surface both, never merge. Single readings unreliable. Educational only; no diagnosis.

calculators.name: Resting Heart Rate Checker
calculators.whyRelevant: Universal vital, wearable-era SEO magnet, feeds the Karvonen target-zone tool; trivial engine fit.

inputs.label: Resting heart rate
inputs.notes: Measure in the morning before getting out of bed (AHA). Count pulse 30 s x 2.

inputs.label: Highly trained / endurance athlete?
inputs.notes: Softens the interpretation of 40-59 bpm.

inputs.label: Age group
inputs.notes: Default adult; pediatric bands from MedlinePlus if the platform wants all-ages support.

calculators.logic: AHA (Target Heart Rates Chart, last reviewed Aug 12, 2024) verbatim: 'For most adults, a resting heart rate between 60 and 100 beats per minute is normal... An athlete or more active person may have a resting heart rate as low as 40 beats per minute.' 'When it comes to resting heart rate, lower is better'; higher resting HR is linked with lower physical fitness, higher blood pressure and higher body weight. MedlinePlus (Pulse, ency 003399) verbatim ranges: newborns 0-1 month 70-190; infants 1-11 months 80-160; 1-2 years 80-130; 3-4 years 80-120; 5-6 years 75-115; 7-9 years 70-110; 10+ and adults 60-100; well-trained athletes 40-60 bpm.

resultCategories.label: Below 60 (adult)
resultCategories.interpretation: Below the typical 60-100 range. In athletes and very active people this can be normal (AHA: as low as 40; MedlinePlus: athletes 40-60).
resultCategories.recommendation: If you are not highly trained, or you feel dizzy, faint or unusually tired, discuss bradycardia with a clinician.

resultCategories.label: Normal (adult)
resultCategories.interpretation: Normal adult resting heart rate (AHA). Lower within this range generally reflects better cardiovascular fitness.
resultCategories.recommendation: Regular aerobic activity tends to lower resting heart rate over time (AHA).

resultCategories.label: Above 100 (adult)
resultCategories.interpretation: Above the normal adult range (tachycardia territory). Stress, anxiety, hormones, caffeine, illness and medication can raise it (AHA lists such factors).
resultCategories.recommendation: Re-check at true rest; a persistently elevated resting heart rate should be discussed with a health care professional (MedlinePlus).

resultCategories.label: Very low (adult)
resultCategories.interpretation: Below even the athlete range cited by AHA/MedlinePlus.
resultCategories.recommendation: Seek medical evaluation, particularly with symptoms.

sources.title: Target Heart Rates Chart (Last Reviewed: Aug 12, 2024) - resting heart rate section
Pulse (Medical Encyclopedia 003399)

calculators.platformMapping: Existing primitives only: numeric bands on restingHr with condition DSL on ageGroup for pediatric band sets; athlete boolean via option points/condition branch adjusts the 40-59 interpretation text. Direction lower-is-better within normal band.
calculators.realWorldPresence: heart.org, MedlinePlus, Cleveland Clinic, every wearable app.
calculators.cautions: Medications (e.g., beta-blockers) alter heart rate (AHA note); do not imply diagnosis of brady/tachycardia; symptomatic advice must direct to care.

calculators.name: Maximum Heart Rate Estimator
calculators.whyRelevant: Feeder value for target-zone tool; classic fitness SEO query; showcases the platform's conflict-surfacing (two formulas).

inputs.label: Age
inputs.notes: Both equations derived in adults; Tanaka cohort healthy adults.

calculators.logic: Two authority formulas, surfaced side by side, never merged: (1) AHA (heart.org Target Heart Rates Chart): 'Your maximum heart rate is about 220 minus your age.' AHA table verbatim: age 20 -> 200 bpm; 30 -> 190; 35 -> 185; 40 -> 180; 45 -> 175; 50 -> 170; 55 -> 165; 60 -> 160; 65 -> 155; 70 -> 150. (2) Tanaka (Tanaka H, Monahan KD, Seals DR. Age-predicted maximal heart rate revisited. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2001 Jan;37(1):153-6; PMID 11153730), abstract verbatim: 'HRmax was strongly related to age (r = -0.90), using the equation of 208 - 0.7 x age'; laboratory cross-validation gave 209 - 0.7 x age; equation 'independent of gender and habitual physical activity status'; the 220-age equation 'underestimates HRmax in older adults.' Mayo Clinic (Exercise intensity, Aug 25, 2023) adopts the Tanaka form: 'multiplying your age by 0.7 and subtracting the total from 208' with worked example age 45 -> 208 - 31.5 = 176.5.

resultCategories.label: Estimated HRmax (220 - age)
resultCategories.interpretation: AHA rule-of-thumb; the figures are averages, to be used as a general guide (AHA).
resultCategories.recommendation: Use as the basis for AHA percent-of-max training zones.

resultCategories.label: Estimated HRmax (Tanaka 208 - 0.7 x age)
resultCategories.interpretation: Meta-analysis-derived equation (18,712 subjects); more accurate in older adults, where 220-age underestimates HRmax (Tanaka 2001).
resultCategories.recommendation: Mayo Clinic uses this form; prefer it for age 50+.

sources.title: Target Heart Rates Chart (220 minus age; age table)
Tanaka H, Monahan KD, Seals DR. Age-predicted maximal heart rate revisited. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2001;37(1):153-6. doi 10.1016/s0735-1097(00)01054-8
Exercise intensity: How to measure it (uses 208 - 0.7 x age)

calculators.platformMapping: Existing primitives only: two derived parameters hrmaxAha = 220 - age and hrmaxTanaka = 208 - 0.7 * age (round()). Dual-output display uses the platform's conflict/attribution pattern; no bands needed.
calculators.realWorldPresence: heart.org chart; Mayo Clinic; CDC formerly; all fitness platforms.
calculators.cautions: Both are population estimates with wide individual spread; medications (e.g., beta-blockers) lower true HRmax (AHA note); people with heart conditions should get targets from their clinician.

calculators.name: Target Heart Rate Zones (AHA % of max + Karvonen HRR)
calculators.whyRelevant: Marquee fitness calculator; pairs resting HR + max HR tools; both methods fully verified from AHA and Mayo.

inputs.label: Resting heart rate (for HRR/Karvonen method)
inputs.notes: Required only when method = hrr.

calculators.logic: Method A - AHA percent of max (heart.org, verbatim): HRmax = 220 - age. 'Target heart rate during moderate-intensity activities is about 50-70% of maximum heart rate. During vigorous physical activity, it's about 70-85% of maximum.' Beginners: start at 50% and build up to 85%. AHA 50-85% zone table verbatim: 20 y -> 100-170 bpm; 30 -> 95-162; 35 -> 93-157; 40 -> 90-153; 45 -> 88-149; 50 -> 85-145; 55 -> 83-140; 60 -> 80-136; 65 -> 78-132; 70 -> 75-128. Method B - HRR/Karvonen (Mayo Clinic, verbatim steps): HRmax = 208 - 0.7 x age; HRR = HRmax - resting HR; target = HRR x intensity% + resting HR. Mayo vigorous bounds: multiply HRR by 0.7 and by 0.85, add resting HR to each. Mayo worked example verbatim: age 45, HRmax 176.5; resting 80 -> HRR 96.5; 96.5 x 0.7 = 67.5, + 80 = 147.5; 96.5 x 0.85 = 82, + 80 = 162; vigorous zone 148-162 bpm rounded. AHA percentage bands (50-70 moderate / 70-85 vigorous) are applied to whichever intensity is selected; Mayo attributes those same percentages to the American Heart Association. Original HRR method citation: Karvonen MJ, Kentala E, Mustala O. The effects of training on heart rate; a longitudinal study. Ann Med Exp Biol Fenn. 1957;35(3):307-15 (PMID 13470504).

resultCategories.label: Moderate-intensity zone
resultCategories.range: 50-70% of HRmax (AHA), or HRR x 0.50-0.70 + resting HR (Karvonen form)
resultCategories.interpretation: Working level for moderate exercise - you can talk but not sing (CDC/Mayo talk-test).
resultCategories.recommendation: Beginners aim for the lower end (50%) and build up gradually (AHA).

resultCategories.label: Vigorous-intensity zone
resultCategories.range: 70-85% of HRmax (AHA), or HRR x 0.70-0.85 + resting HR (Mayo)
resultCategories.interpretation: Vigorous training zone; can't say more than a few words without pausing for breath.
resultCategories.recommendation: If heart rate exceeds the zone you are straining - slow down; if below and effort feels light, push a little harder (AHA).

resultCategories.label: Above zone
resultCategories.interpretation: Above target - overexertion risk.
resultCategories.recommendation: Reduce intensity (AHA).

sources.title: Target Heart Rates Chart (50-70% moderate, 70-85% vigorous, 220-age, age table)
Exercise intensity: How to measure it (HRR method steps + worked example; attributes 50-70/70-85% to AHA)
Karvonen MJ, Kentala E, Mustala O. The effects of training on heart rate; a longitudinal study. Ann Med Exp Biol Fenn. 1957;35(3):307-15

calculators.platformMapping: Existing primitives only: derived hrmax (per method: 220-age or 208-0.7*age via condition DSL on method), derived hrr = hrmax - restingHr, derived zoneLow/zoneHigh = method==hrr ? round(hrr*pLow + restingHr) : round(hrmax*pLow) with pLow/pHigh from option points on intensity. Ternary + round() suffice. Output is a numeric range (two derived values), not a scored category - platform must render dual-number results, which it already does for derived parameters.
calculators.realWorldPresence: heart.org chart, Mayo Clinic calculator guidance, CDC (retired page), every fitness tracker.
calculators.cautions: Medications lower max HR and target zone - users on heart medication must ask their clinician for targets (AHA verbatim caution). CDC's retired page used different %HRmax cutoffs (64-76%/77-93%); not shown because it could not be re-verified (see openIssues).

calculators.name: Non-HDL Cholesterol
calculators.whyRelevant: Directly computable from any lab report (TC - HDL); Mayo and MedlinePlus both endorse it as a preferred risk marker - ideal for the lab-report lead-magnet.

inputs.label: Age
inputs.notes: Selects the <=19 vs 20+ band set (MedlinePlus).

inputs.label: Non-HDL cholesterol (computed)
inputs.notes: nonHdl = totalCholesterol - hdl

calculators.logic: Formula (Mayo, MedlinePlus): non-HDL = total cholesterol - HDL cholesterol; it 'includes all the bad types of cholesterol.' Mayo verbatim: 'An optimal level of non-HDL cholesterol for most people is less than 130 milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL), which is 3.37 millimoles per liter (mmol/L). For people with a history of heart attack, the desired level may be lower. Higher numbers mean a higher risk of heart disease.' MedlinePlus healthy-level table verbatim: age 19 or younger: non-HDL less than 120 mg/dL; men 20+: less than 130 mg/dL; women 20+: less than 130 mg/dL. Mayo states non-HDL 'may be more useful than calculating your cholesterol ratio' and both beat total cholesterol or LDL alone for risk prediction.

resultCategories.label: Optimal (age <=19)
resultCategories.interpretation: Within the MedlinePlus healthy level for age 19 or younger.
resultCategories.recommendation: Maintain heart-healthy diet and activity habits.

resultCategories.label: Optimal (age 20+)
resultCategories.interpretation: Optimal for most people (Mayo, MedlinePlus).
resultCategories.recommendation: Keep up heart-healthy habits; people with prior heart attack may need a lower target - follow their clinician's goal (Mayo).

resultCategories.interpretation: Higher numbers mean a higher risk of heart disease (Mayo). No finer public consumer grading of non-HDL is published by the cited sources.
resultCategories.recommendation: Review the full lipid panel with a clinician; lifestyle change first-line, treatment per clinician judgment.

calculators.name: Cholesterol Ratios (TC/HDL primary; LDL/HDL & TG/HDL secondary, research-context)
calculators.whyRelevant: Printed on many lab reports; heavy search volume; calculation and qualitative interpretation are fetch-verified (Mayo) even though the popular numeric cutoffs are not.

inputs.label: TC/HDL ratio (computed)
inputs.notes: ratio = totalCholesterol / hdl; unit-independent when both are in the same unit

calculators.logic: Mayo verbatim: 'To calculate your cholesterol ratio, divide your total cholesterol number by your HDL cholesterol number. So if your total cholesterol is 200 mg/dL (5.2 mmol/L) and your HDL is 50 mg/dL (1.3 mmol/L), your ratio would be 4-to-1. Higher ratios mean a higher risk of heart disease.' Mayo adds that non-HDL is now considered the more useful marker. Popular numeric cutoffs (ratio under 5 considered normal; about 3.5-to-1 very good/ideal) appear in search results attributed to Cleveland Clinic and Univ. of Rochester content but could NOT be fetch-verified on an allowed domain today - display them only with an explicit weak-source flag or omit (see openIssues). Research context: higher TC/HDL ratio associated with higher mortality risk in general-population cohort (PMC9797665).

resultCategories.label: Lower ratio
resultCategories.range: e.g., 3.5-4.0 or below (illustrative; no fetch-verified authority cutoff)
resultCategories.interpretation: Lower ratios mean lower estimated heart-disease risk (Mayo: higher ratios mean a higher risk).
resultCategories.recommendation: Keep up heart-healthy habits; interpret alongside non-HDL cholesterol, which Mayo considers more useful.

resultCategories.label: Higher ratio
resultCategories.range: Above ~5:1 (commonly quoted, weakly sourced - flag in UI)
resultCategories.interpretation: Higher ratios mean a higher risk of heart disease (Mayo).
resultCategories.recommendation: Review the full lipid panel with a clinician; lifestyle measures first-line.

mergedFrom.name: LDL / HDL Ratio
mergedFrom.whyRelevant: Occasionally requested lab-report ratio, but no major consumer authority publishes interpretation cutoffs - research-context only.
mergedFrom.logic: ratio = LDL / HDL (unit-independent, same units). No CDC/NIH/AHA/Mayo/Cleveland consumer page publishes LDL/HDL interpretation categories (verified by targeted search 2026-08-20). Peer-reviewed cohorts associate higher LDL/HDL with coronary atherosclerosis, carotid plaque, first stroke in hypertensive patients, and NAFLD (PMC9206383, PMC9700971, PMC12460095, PMC7993485) but use study-specific cutoffs - no universal threshold.

resultCategories.label: Computed ratio (research context)
resultCategories.interpretation: Higher LDL/HDL ratios are associated in research cohorts with higher atherosclerotic risk; no authoritative consumer categories exist.
resultCategories.recommendation: Interpret LDL and HDL individually against guideline levels (see measurements) and discuss with a clinician; prefer non-HDL or TC/HDL for report-level context.

mergedFrom.name: Triglyceride / HDL Ratio
mergedFrom.whyRelevant: Popular insulin-resistance proxy with real peer-reviewed support, but explicitly lacking a universal cutoff - honest tiering keeps it out of the launch set.

inputs.label: TG/HDL ratio (computed, mg/dL basis)
inputs.notes: CRITICAL: published cutoffs are mg/dL-based. A ratio computed from mmol/L values must be multiplied by 2.290 (= 88.57/38.67 inverse relationship) to compare; engine must convert both inputs to mg/dL before dividing.

mergedFrom.logic: ratio = TG(mg/dL) / HDL(mg/dL). Review (Kosmas CE et al. The Triglyceride/High-Density Lipoprotein Cholesterol (TG/HDL-C) Ratio as a Risk Marker for Metabolic Syndrome and Cardiovascular Disease. Diagnostics. 2023;13(5):929; PMC10001260): correlates with insulin resistance, central obesity, metabolic syndrome and CVD; proposed cutoffs vary widely - general population >2.75 (men) / >1.65 (women) 'highly predictive of MetS as well as of a first coronary event'; US ethnic variation approximately 3.0 (non-Hispanic whites/Mexican Americans) vs 2.0 (non-Hispanic blacks); review verbatim: 'the absence of a universal cut-off value renders its use as a predicting biomarker for CVD somewhat challenging.' 40-year cohort (PMC6913120): highest-quartile ratio >1.8 associated with insulin resistance and CVD (HR 1.47, 95% CI 1.26-1.93).

resultCategories.label: Computed ratio (research context)
resultCategories.interpretation: Higher TG/HDL ratios are associated with insulin resistance and cardiometabolic risk in research cohorts; cutoffs differ by sex and ethnicity and no universal threshold exists (Kosmas 2023).
resultCategories.recommendation: Treat as a conversation-starter, not a diagnosis; interpret triglycerides and HDL individually against guideline levels and discuss metabolic risk screening with a clinician.

calculators.name: ASCVD 10-Year Risk (Pooled Cohort Equations, 2013 ACC/AHA)
calculators.whyRelevant: The definitive US primary-prevention risk score and the natural upgrade path from the existing modified-Framingham tool - but it is blocked on missing engine primitives (ln, exp) and a coefficient dataset, so it cannot ship in the current engine.

inputs.label: Age
inputs.notes: PCE 'valid for those aged 40-79 years of age' (2018 guideline synopsis, PMC6946888); MDCalc implementation restricts to 40-75 (the statin-decision window). Record both; UI should use 40-79 with a 40-75 note for statin framing.

inputs.label: Total cholesterol
inputs.notes: 130-320 bound per ACC Risk Estimator Plus implementation (blocked-cited).

inputs.label: HDL cholesterol
inputs.notes: 20-100 bound per ACC implementation (blocked-cited).

inputs.label: Systolic blood pressure
inputs.notes: 90-200 bound per ACC implementation (blocked-cited).

calculators.logic: SCOPE DOCUMENTATION (do not implement in current engine): Risk = 1 - S0(10)^exp(IndividualSum - MeanSum), where IndividualSum is a sex- and race-specific linear combination of natural-log-transformed continuous terms - ln(age), ln(age)^2 (women), ln(total cholesterol), ln(HDL-C), ln(treated or untreated systolic BP) - plus smoker, diabetes indicators and ln-age interaction terms; S0(10) is the group-specific 10-year baseline survival. Four coefficient sets: White women, African American women, White men, African American men. WHERE THE FULL COEFFICIENT TABLES LIVE: Goff DC Jr, Lloyd-Jones DM, Bennett G, et al. 2013 ACC/AHA guideline on the assessment of cardiovascular risk. Circulation. 2014 Jun 24;129(25 Suppl 2):S49-73. doi 10.1161/01.cir.0000437741.48606.98 (PMID 24222018, citation fetch-verified; free full text at ahajournals.org, which 403-blocks automated fetch) - equation parameters and worked examples are in the guideline's appendix tables ('Equation Parameters of the Pooled Cohort Equations' + baseline survival, Appendix 7 / Tables A-B of the online supplement; blocked-cited). Secondary implementation references: MDCalc 'ASCVD (Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease) 2013 Risk Calculator from AHA/ACC' (calc/3398, inputs and age bounds fetch-verified) and ACC Risk Estimator Plus (tools.acc.org, JS app, blocked-cited). Outcome definition (MDCalc, fetch-verified): 10-year risk of hard ASCVD = myocardial infarction, stroke, or death due to coronary heart disease or stroke. RISK CATEGORIES (2018 AHA/ACC Cholesterol Guideline via ASPC synopsis PMC6946888, fetch-verified): Low <5%; Borderline 5-<7.5%; Intermediate 7.5-<20%; High >=20%.

resultCategories.interpretation: Low 10-year risk of hard ASCVD events.
resultCategories.recommendation: Guideline: lifestyle only - emphasize heart-healthy lifestyle; statin generally not indicated absent risk-enhancing factors.

resultCategories.interpretation: Borderline 10-year risk.
resultCategories.recommendation: Guideline: risk-enhancing factors (e.g., family history, persistent LDL-C elevation) may favor moderate-intensity statin after clinician discussion; coronary artery calcium scoring can refine the decision.

resultCategories.label: Intermediate risk
resultCategories.interpretation: Intermediate 10-year risk.
resultCategories.recommendation: Guideline: moderate-intensity statin should be considered after shared decision-making; CAC scoring may refine.

resultCategories.label: High risk
resultCategories.interpretation: High 10-year risk.
resultCategories.recommendation: Guideline: statin therapy to reduce LDL-C at least 50% plus lifestyle therapy; managed by a clinician.

calculators.platformMapping: ENGINE CAPABILITY AVAILABLE: engine v1 supports ln(), exp(), finite pow(), derived formulas, condition branches, and result bands, so the PCE mathematical shape is structurally expressible. The four sex/race coefficient sets, baseline survival and mean terms, current PCE-versus-PREVENT product choice, source verification, applicability, and clinical review remain unresolved; do not author or publish from this research row.
calculators.realWorldPresence: ACC Risk Estimator Plus (tools.acc.org), MDCalc, AHA CV Risk Calculator, embedded in every US EHR.
calculators.cautions: Clinician-oriented tool: statin recommendations must be framed as guideline information, not personal advice. Validated only for ages 40-79 without prior ASCVD and LDL-C <190 mg/dL (per guideline framing on MDCalc: LDL 70-189 mg/dL); 'Other' race estimates are less reliable (guideline caveat). Known to overestimate in some modern cohorts; AHA released PREVENT (2023) as successor - consider documenting PREVENT before committing engineering work on ln/exp for PCE alone.

calculators.name: HOMA-IR (Homeostatic Model Assessment of Insulin Resistance)
calculators.whyRelevant: Directly computable from two common lab-report values (fasting glucose + fasting insulin); flagship insulin-resistance metric for a lab-report/wellness lead magnet and complements Niro CWS biomarkers.

inputs.label: Fasting plasma glucose
inputs.notes: Fasting (>=8 h). mmol/L->mg/dL factor 18.016 is the standard glucose molar-mass constant (MW 180.16); confirm against an ADA/AHA SI conversion table before shipping (see openIssues).

inputs.label: Fasting insulin
inputs.notes: uU/mL is identical to mU/L. Do NOT enable pmol/L until the conversion factor conflict (6.00 vs 6.945 pmol/L per uU/mL) is resolved from an authoritative table — see openIssues.

calculators.logic: HOMA-IR = fasting glucose (mg/dL) x fasting insulin (uU/mL or mU/L) / 405. SI form: HOMA-IR = fasting glucose (mmol/L) x fasting insulin (uU/mL) / 22.5. Verbatim from PMC8693111: "HOMA-IR = glucose (mg/dL) x insulin (mU/L)/405". Verbatim from Gutch et al 2015 (PMC4287763): "IRHOMA = (I0 x G0)/ 22.5" where I0 = fasting plasma insulin (uU/mL), G0 = fasting plasma glucose (mmol/L). The two forms are algebraically identical (405 = 22.5 x 18.016... note 22.5 x 18 = 405, i.e. the 405 constant embeds the rounded factor 18). Model is calibrated so a healthy nondiabetic individual is approximately 1 (PMC8693111: "for healthy nondiabetic individuals, the ideal HOMA-IR value should be around 1").
calculators.outputScale: Unitless ratio; typical outputs roughly 0.3–15; higher = more insulin resistant.

resultCategories.label: Around 1 (approximately <1.5)
resultCategories.interpretation: Near the model's calibration point for healthy nondiabetic adults (ideal value around 1 per PMC8693111).
resultCategories.recommendation: No action suggested by this index alone; maintain healthy diet, activity, and weight.

resultCategories.label: Intermediate / no universal cutoff zone
resultCategories.interpretation: Below the NHANES research cutoff. There is NO universal HOMA-IR cutoff; NHANES III median in US adults without diabetes was 2.2, and literature cutoffs range roughly 1.5–3 (PMC8693111); Asian-population cutoffs range 1.4–2.5 (MDCalc).
resultCategories.recommendation: Interpret alongside glucose, A1C, lipids, and waist circumference; recheck periodically if other metabolic risk factors are present.

resultCategories.label: Consistent with insulin resistance (research cutoffs)
resultCategories.interpretation: Meets the >=2.5 cutoff used in NHANES to indicate insulin resistance; values between 2.0 and 3.0 are commonly used in U.S. clinical and research settings (MDCalc, verbatim).
resultCategories.recommendation: Discuss with a healthcare provider; guideline-consistent next steps are diabetes/prediabetes screening (FPG, A1C, or OGTT) and lifestyle measures. Not a diagnosis.

calculators.platformMapping: Fully expressible today: derived parameter formula (glucose_mgdl * insulin_uUml / 405) using whitelisted * and /; unit conversion factors for mmol/L; category bands with min-inclusive control on the derived value (higher-is-worse direction). No missing primitives.
calculators.realWorldPresence: MDCalc; ubiquitous on lab-interpretation/wellness platforms (mdapp.co, backtable.com, healthmatters.io observed in search); standard in metabolic research (NHANES analyses).
calculators.cautions: Not valid for people on insulin therapy or with type 1 diabetes; insulin assays are not standardized between labs; NOT a diagnostic test and has no universal cutoff — UI must label each threshold with its source (NHANES research cutoff vs common clinical range vs Asian-population range); requires true fasting sample. Public-domain formula, no licensing restrictions.

mergedFrom.name: QUICKI (Quantitative Insulin Sensitivity Check Index)
mergedFrom.whyRelevant: Same two inputs as HOMA-IR (natural companion output on one page), better correlation with clamp in some settings; secondary because it duplicates HOMA-IR's inputs/answer and requires a new engine primitive.

inputs.label: Fasting insulin
inputs.notes: Must be > 0 (log). Same pmol/L conversion caution as HOMA-IR.

inputs.label: Fasting plasma glucose
inputs.notes: Formula is defined with glucose in mg/dL.

mergedFrom.logic: QUICKI = 1 / [log(I0) + log(G0)] where I0 = fasting insulin (uU/mL) and G0 = fasting glucose (mg/dL); log is base 10. Verbatim from MDCalc journal review: "1/[log(I0) + log(G0)]", "I0- Fasting insulin uU/mL", "G0- Fasting glucose in mg/dL". Original: Katz A et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2000;85(7):2402-2410 (doi:10.1210/JCEM.85.7.6661); correlated with clamp-derived insulin sensitivity at r = 0.78 in the validation study; meta-analysis r = 0.61 (95% CI 0.55-0.65).
mergedFrom.outputScale: Unitless; typical human range roughly 0.25–0.45; HIGHER = more insulin sensitive (lower-is-worse for risk).

resultCategories.label: Consistent with insulin resistance
resultCategories.interpretation: Below the "most commonly cited threshold for insulin resistance" of <0.357 (MDCalc journal review, verbatim).
resultCategories.recommendation: Discuss with a healthcare provider; consider guideline-based diabetes screening and lifestyle measures. Not a diagnosis.

resultCategories.label: Around normal insulin sensitivity
resultCategories.interpretation: At/above the common insulin-resistance threshold; normal fasting QUICKI values were approximately 0.366 (SD +/- 0.029) (MDCalc journal review, verbatim). Higher QUICKI = greater insulin sensitivity.
resultCategories.recommendation: No action suggested by this index alone; maintain healthy lifestyle.

mergedFrom.platformMapping: MISSING PRIMITIVE: requires log10() — not in the whitelisted expression set (+ - * / min max round abs pow, ternary). Everything else maps to existing primitives (derived formula + category bands with lower-is-worse direction). Recommend adding log10() and ln() together (also unblocks TyG).

mergedFrom.cautions: Same fasting/assay caveats as HOMA-IR; not for insulin-treated patients; log base must be 10 (a natural-log implementation silently produces wrong values); no universal cutoff — 0.357 is a commonly cited research threshold, not a diagnostic criterion. Public-domain formula.

calculators.mergeNote: QUICKI (log10-gated) is a secondary output computed from the same two inputs (see mergedFrom).

calculators.name: FINDRISC (Finnish Diabetes Risk Score)
calculators.whyRelevant: Best-validated no-lab 10-year type 2 diabetes risk questionnaire; international counterpart to the platform's existing IDRS; strong SEO demand and pure self-service inputs.

inputs.label: Body mass index (derived from height and weight, or entered directly)
inputs.notes: Bands: <25 = 0 pts; 25–30 = 1 pt; >30 = 3 pts (PMC6887494 verbatim: "<25, 0; 25–30, 1; >30, 3 points"). MDCalc renders the middle band as 25–29.9 — boundary at exactly 30.0 differs between mirrors; see conflicts/openIssues.

inputs.label: Waist circumference (measured below the ribs, usually at navel level)
inputs.notes: Sex-branched bands. Men: <94 cm = 0; 94–102 = 3; >102 = 4. Women: <80 cm = 0; 80–88 = 3; >88 = 4 (PMC6887494 verbatim).

inputs.label: Sex
inputs.notes: Carries no points itself; drives the waist-circumference branch.

inputs.label: Do you get at least 30 minutes of physical activity daily (at work and/or leisure)?
inputs.notes: PMC6887494 verbatim: ">=30 min/day, 0; <30 min/day, 2 points". MDCalc phrases the same item as >=4 hr/week vs <4 hr/week — wording variant, same points.

inputs.label: Do you eat vegetables, fruit, or berries every day?
Have you ever taken medication for high blood pressure?
Have you ever been found to have high blood glucose (e.g., in a health exam, during illness, or pregnancy)?
Family history of diabetes (type 1 or type 2)

options.label: Yes: grandparent, aunt, uncle, or first cousin (but no first-degree relative)
Yes: parent, brother, sister, or own child

inputs.notes: PMC6887494 verbatim: "no, 0; second-degree but no first-degree relative, 3; first-degree relative, 5 points".

calculators.logic: Sum of all item points. Score range 0–26. Full point table (verbatim, PMC6887494 / HUNT, matching Lindström & Tuomilehto 2003): Age (years): "<45, 0; 45–54, 2; 55–64, 3; and >=65, 4 points". BMI (kg/m2): "<25, 0; 25–30, 1; >30, 3 points". Waist (cm) men: "<94, 0; 94–102, 3; >102, 4 points"; women: "<80, 0; 80–88, 3; >88, 4 points". Physical activity: ">=30 min/day, 0; <30 min/day, 2 points". Fruit/vegetables: "yes, 0; no, 1 point". Antihypertensive medication: "no, 0; yes, 2 points". High blood glucose history: "no, 0; yes, 5 points". Family history: "no, 0; second-degree but no first-degree relative, 3; first-degree relative, 5 points". Independent MDCalc mirror agrees on every point value (age rendered as >64 = 4; BMI middle band as 25–29.9).
calculators.outputScale: Integer 0–26; higher = higher 10-year risk of type 2 diabetes.

resultCategories.label: Low risk
resultCategories.interpretation: Estimated ~1 in 100 will develop type 2 diabetes within 10 years (standard FINDRISC form categories; PMC9709506 lists 0–6 as low risk).
resultCategories.recommendation: Maintain healthy weight, daily activity, and vegetable/fruit intake.

resultCategories.label: Slightly elevated risk
resultCategories.interpretation: Estimated ~4% (about 1 in 25) 10-year risk (PMC9709506: "7-11: Elevated risk (4%)", citing Schwarz 2009 JCEM).
resultCategories.recommendation: Adopt weight management and regular physical activity; recheck risk periodically.

resultCategories.label: Moderate risk
resultCategories.interpretation: Estimated ~16.66% (about 1 in 6) 10-year risk (PMC9709506).
resultCategories.recommendation: Lifestyle change is warranted; consider discussing blood glucose testing with a healthcare provider.

resultCategories.label: High risk
resultCategories.interpretation: Estimated ~33% (about 1 in 3) 10-year risk (PMC9709506).
resultCategories.recommendation: See a healthcare provider for blood glucose testing (FPG/A1C/OGTT) and structured lifestyle-prevention support.

resultCategories.label: Very high risk
resultCategories.interpretation: Estimated ~50% (about 1 in 2) 10-year risk (PMC9709506).
resultCategories.recommendation: See a healthcare provider promptly for blood glucose testing and diabetes-prevention intervention.
