calculators.platformMapping: condition DSL branches on sex, age band (male <20 vs >=20; female <18 vs >=18) and group; derived formula b0 + b1*age + b2*pow(age,2) + b3*pow(height,2), then *60 for L/min - all within whitelisted math (+ - * / pow). LLN = same expression with the LLN height coefficient (a second derived parameter). Percent-predicted = division. Zones = category bands (higher-is-better) on percent of personal best/predicted. Unit conversion in->cm factor 2.54. NO missing primitives for Hankinson. MISSING PRIMITIVES flagged for alternatives: Nunn & Gregg 1989 requires exp() and ln(); GLI-2012 requires exp/ln plus large spline/LMS lookup tables.
calculators.realWorldPresence: MDCalc (Estimated/Expected Peak Expiratory Flow), Medscape Reference calculator, QxMD, Guideline Central, EBMcalc - all built on Hankinson/NHANES III (adults) and related pediatric equations.
calculators.cautions: Race-specific reference equations are increasingly discouraged in favor of race-neutral GLI equations (see openIssues) - display a transparent note and never hard-require race. Predicted PEF is population-average; personal best is the preferred asthma-management anchor (StatPearls zones are defined against personal best). Not a diagnostic tool; peak-flow technique/effort strongly affects readings. Output unit conversion (L/s -> L/min) must be shown explicitly.

calculators.name: FEV1/FVC Ratio & Airflow Obstruction Interpreter (GOLD vs ATS/ERS)
calculators.whyRelevant: Home spirometers increasingly report FEV1/FVC; users want the GOLD interpretation. Also completes the spirometry cluster with the Hankinson %-predicted engine already needed for PEF. Tier 2 because inputs come from a device/test rather than pure self-report.

inputs.label: Values measured after bronchodilator?
inputs.notes: GOLD COPD definition requires POST-bronchodilator values; if false, show a caveat instead of a COPD-pattern statement.

inputs.label: FEV1/FVC (computed)
inputs.notes: ratio = fev1 / fvc

calculators.logic: RATIO: ratio = FEV1/FVC. GOLD DEFINITION (StatPearls, verbatim): COPD is defined spirometrically by a 'postbronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC) ratio less than 0.70'. GOLD SEVERITY (FEV1 % predicted, ratio < 0.7): Grade 1 (Mild) FEV1 >= 80%; Grade 2 (Moderate) 50-79%; Grade 3 (Severe) 30-49%; Grade 4 (Very severe) < 30%. FEV1 % predicted computed with Hankinson adult FEV1 equations (form b0 + b1*age + b2*age^2 + b3*height^2, height cm, result L; verbatim adult coefficients, PRD/LLN height terms): MALE >= 20y - Caucasian 0.5536, -0.01303, -0.000172, 0.00014098 (LLN 0.00011607); African-American 0.3411, -0.02309, (no age^2), 0.00013194 (LLN 0.00010561); Mexican-American 0.6306, -0.02928, (no age^2), 0.00015104 (LLN 0.00012670). FEMALE >= 18y - Caucasian 0.4333, -0.00361, -0.000194, 0.00011496 (LLN 0.00009283); African-American 0.3433, -0.01283, -0.000097, 0.00010846 (LLN 0.00008546); Mexican-American 0.4529, -0.01178, -0.000113, 0.00012154 (LLN 0.00009890). FVC adult coefficients (same form): Male Caucasian -0.1933, 0.00064, -0.000269, 0.00018642 (LLN 0.00015695); Male African-American -0.1517, -0.01821, (none), 0.00016643 (LLN 0.00013670); Male Mexican-American 0.2376, -0.00891, -0.000182, 0.00017823 (LLN 0.00014947); Female Caucasian -0.3560, 0.01870, -0.000382, 0.00014815 (LLN 0.00012198); Female African-American -0.3039, 0.00536, -0.000265, 0.00013606 (LLN 0.00010916); Female Mexican-American 0.1210, 0.00307, -0.000237, 0.00014246 (LLN 0.00011570). CONFLICT (must be surfaced, not merged) - ERS/ATS 2022 standard defines 'airflow limitation by an FEV1/FVC ratio that is 1.645z below the mean, which is approximately the 5th percentile' (LLN), and grades severity by FEV1 z-score: 'z-score > -1.645 as normal, z-scores between -1.65 and -2.5 as mild impairment, z-scores between -2.5 and -4 as moderate impairment, and z-scores <-4 as severe impairment'. StatPearls also notes: 'The lower limit of normal (the fifth percentile of the reference population) may be preferred in patients older than 70 to avoid overdiagnosis due to normal age-related decline in forced vital capacity.'
calculators.outputScale: Ratio 0-1 (display 2 dp); FEV1 % predicted 0-150%; GOLD grade 1-4 when obstruction pattern present.

resultCategories.label: No airflow obstruction pattern (by GOLD fixed ratio)
resultCategories.interpretation: Your ratio is at or above the GOLD fixed threshold, so a COPD-pattern obstruction is not suggested by this ratio alone. Restrictive patterns cannot be excluded by ratio alone.
resultCategories.recommendation: If you have respiratory symptoms (breathlessness, chronic cough, wheeze) despite a normal ratio, discuss full pulmonary function testing with your clinician.

resultCategories.label: Airflow obstruction pattern - GOLD 1 (Mild)
resultCategories.interpretation: Pattern consistent with mild airflow obstruction under GOLD criteria.
resultCategories.recommendation: Share these values with your clinician for confirmation with quality-assured spirometry; if you smoke, quitting is the most effective intervention.

resultCategories.label: Airflow obstruction pattern - GOLD 2 (Moderate)
resultCategories.interpretation: Pattern consistent with moderate airflow obstruction under GOLD criteria.
resultCategories.recommendation: Arrange clinical review; confirmatory spirometry and symptom/exacerbation assessment guide treatment.

resultCategories.label: Airflow obstruction pattern - GOLD 3 (Severe)
resultCategories.interpretation: Pattern consistent with severe airflow obstruction under GOLD criteria.
resultCategories.recommendation: Seek clinical review promptly; do not adjust medication without professional guidance.

resultCategories.label: Airflow obstruction pattern - GOLD 4 (Very severe)
resultCategories.interpretation: Pattern consistent with very severe airflow obstruction under GOLD criteria.
resultCategories.recommendation: Seek medical care promptly, particularly if you have worsening breathlessness, low oxygen readings, or signs of an exacerbation.

calculators.platformMapping: derived parameters: ratio = fev1/fvc; predictedFEV1 via condition-DSL-branched polynomial (pow); percentPredicted = fev1/predictedFEV1*100. GOLD staging = nested category bands (band on ratio with min-exclusive 0.70 edge, then bands on percentPredicted 80/50/30 cutoffs, lower-is-worse direction). Post-bronchodilator flag = condition DSL gating the interpretation text. MISSING PRIMITIVES: ATS/ERS z-score pathway needs GLI-2012 reference (spline/LMS lookup tables + exp/ln) - flag as unimplementable today; ship GOLD fixed-ratio with the ATS/ERS conflict displayed verbatim.
calculators.realWorldPresence: GOLD staging calculators on MDCalc (GOLD criteria for COPD), QxMD, Medscape; NIOSH offers an NHANES III spirometry reference calculator (training use).
calculators.cautions: Requires spirometry-quality measurements - home devices vary; never present output as a COPD diagnosis (diagnosis requires post-bronchodilator, quality-assured spirometry plus clinical assessment). Fixed 0.70 ratio over-diagnoses obstruction in older adults and under-diagnoses in younger - show the ATS/ERS LLN/z-score position as a labeled conflict. Race-specific reference equations carry the same caveat as the PEF calculator.

calculators.name: Respiratory Rate Checker (Adult)
calculators.whyRelevant: Zero-equipment vital-sign self-check that pairs with SpO2 and heart-rate content; strong SEO ('normal breathing rate'). Simple band logic; authorities differ slightly on the normal range, which the platform surfaces.

inputs.label: Breaths counted
inputs.notes: Instruct: count at rest, ideally while the person is unaware, for a full 60 seconds (or 30 seconds x 2).

inputs.label: Breaths per minute (computed)
inputs.notes: rate = breathsCounted * (60 / countDuration)

calculators.logic: rate = breathsCounted * (60/countDuration). REFERENCE RANGES (record ALL, labeled by org - platform surfaces conflicts): StatPearls (Vital Sign Assessment, verbatim): 'The respiratory rate is the number of breaths/min, with a normal adult range of 12 to 20'; bradypnea < 12 breaths/min; tachypnea > 20 breaths/min. MedlinePlus (Rapid shallow breathing, verbatim): 'A normal breathing rate for an adult at rest is 12 to 20 breaths per minute.' MedlinePlus (Vital signs encyclopedia page): breathing '12 to 18 breaths per minute'. Cleveland Clinic (verbatim): 'The normal respiratory rate for an adult at rest is 12 to 18 breaths per minute' and 'A respiration rate under 12 or over 25 breaths per minute while resting may be a sign of an underlying health condition.'
calculators.outputScale: breaths per minute, integer

resultCategories.label: Below typical range (bradypnea)
resultCategories.interpretation: Slower than the adult resting range cited by StatPearls, MedlinePlus and Cleveland Clinic; can occur with sedation, some medications, or medical conditions.
resultCategories.recommendation: If this is persistent, or accompanied by drowsiness, confusion or blue lips, seek medical care promptly.

resultCategories.label: Typical adult resting range
resultCategories.range: 12-18 breaths/min (all cited authorities agree); 19-20 normal per StatPearls/MedlinePlus but upper-borderline per Cleveland Clinic/MedlinePlus vital-signs page
resultCategories.interpretation: Within the adult resting range. Note the labeled inter-source difference for 19-20 breaths/min.
resultCategories.recommendation: No action needed for an isolated normal reading. Recheck when relaxed if you were active or anxious.

resultCategories.label: Above typical range (tachypnea)
resultCategories.interpretation: Faster than the adult resting range; fever, anxiety, pain, lung or heart conditions can raise it.
resultCategories.recommendation: Recheck at rest. Seek medical care if elevated breathing is persistent or comes with chest pain, breathlessness at rest, bluish lips/skin, or fever (per MedlinePlus emergency guidance).

calculators.platformMapping: derived parameter (multiplication) for the 30s->60s conversion; numeric bands with min-inclusive edges for <12 / 12-20 / >20; the 12-18 vs 12-20 disagreement rendered via the platform's per-org conflict display, not merged. NO missing primitives.
calculators.realWorldPresence: Cleveland Clinic and MedlinePlus publish the ranges; American Lung Association and hospital patient-education pages describe self-counting; few standalone calculators exist, making this an easy differentiator.
calculators.cautions: Adult-only (pediatric ranges differ sharply by age - would need an age-banded table and separate pediatric sources before extending). Counting your own breaths alters the rate; recommend having someone else count. Not for emergency triage.

calculators.name: Blood Oxygen (SpO2) Reading Checker
calculators.whyRelevant: Pulse oximeters and smartwatches put SpO2 in every home; 'is 94 oxygen level ok' is a high-volume query. Three trusted authorities give slightly different action thresholds - exactly the conflict-surfacing this platform is built for.

inputs.label: SpO2 reading
inputs.notes: Instruct user to re-take the reading (NHS: retake immediately if <=92; recheck within an hour if 93-94) with a warm, still hand and no nail polish.

inputs.label: Pregnant or recently given birth?
inputs.notes: NHS applies a stricter 94% threshold in pregnancy.

inputs.label: Known chronic lung disease (e.g. COPD)?
inputs.notes: Cleveland Clinic: 'If you have a lung disease such as COPD or pneumonia, your normal oxygen saturation level may be lower.' Personal target should come from the treating clinician.

calculators.logic: REFERENCE VALUES (all verbatim, labeled by org - surface, never merge): WHO (Pulse Oximetry Training Manual, 2011): 'A healthy individual with normal lungs, breathing air at sea level, will have an arterial oxygen saturation of 95% - 100%'; 'If the oxygen saturation is 94% or lower, the patient is hypoxic and needs to be treated quickly. A saturation of less than 90% is a clinical emergency.' (anaesthesia/monitoring context). NHS England (home pulse-oximetry leaflet, verbatim chart): 100-95 = 'Normal blood oxygen level for most people - stay at home and continue to check your blood oxygen level regularly'; 94 or 93 (re-take within an hour first) = 'contact NHS 111 or your GP as soon as possible'; '92% or less' (retake immediately first) = 'attend your nearest A&E immediately or call 999'; pregnancy: 'If your blood oxygen levels are 94% or less, you should contact your hospital immediately or call 999.' Cleveland Clinic (verbatim): 'For most people, a normal pulse oximeter reading for your oxygen saturation level is between 95% and 100%'; 'If you're using an oximeter at home and your oxygen saturation level is 92% or lower, call your healthcare provider. If it's at 88% or lower, get to the nearest emergency room as soon as possible.' Accuracy notes: Cleveland Clinic 'Your actual blood saturation level may be 2% to 4% higher or lower than what the oximeter reads'; NHS: oximeters 'may be less accurate if you have brown or black skin. They may show readings higher than the level of oxygen in your blood.' StatPearls: 'A normal SpO2 in healthy adults is 95% to 100%.'
calculators.outputScale: % saturation, bands 50-100

resultCategories.label: Normal
resultCategories.interpretation: Within the normal range cited by WHO, NHS, Cleveland Clinic and StatPearls.
resultCategories.recommendation: No action needed for an isolated normal reading. Recheck if you feel more unwell - symptoms matter more than a single number.

resultCategories.label: Borderline low - recheck and seek advice
resultCategories.interpretation: NHS: contact 111/GP as soon as possible if it remains 93-94% on recheck within an hour. WHO regards <=94% as hypoxic in monitored settings. Cleveland Clinic does not trigger its call-provider threshold until <=92%. (Conflict shown, both labeled.)
resultCategories.recommendation: Re-take the reading after resting; if it stays 93-94% contact your doctor or urgent-care line promptly (NHS guidance). Pregnant users: treat 94% or less as urgent - contact your hospital immediately or call 999 (NHS).

resultCategories.label: Low - urgent action
resultCategories.interpretation: NHS: 92% or less warrants immediate A&E/999 after an immediate retake. Cleveland Clinic: at <=92% call your healthcare provider; ER at <=88%. WHO: below 90% is a clinical emergency. (All labeled.)
resultCategories.recommendation: Re-take immediately; if still at this level, seek emergency care per NHS/WHO guidance - do not wait, even without breathlessness ('Even if you do not feel breathless, your oxygen levels may be low' - NHS).

resultCategories.label: Very low - emergency
resultCategories.interpretation: Below every cited action threshold (Cleveland Clinic ER threshold 88%; WHO <90% clinical emergency; NHS <=92% A&E/999).
resultCategories.recommendation: Seek emergency care now (999/911/A&E).

calculators.platformMapping: numeric bands (min-inclusive edges at 95, 93, 89) with lower-is-worse direction; condition DSL branches for pregnancy (94% threshold override) and chronic-lung-disease messaging; per-org conflict display for the 92-vs-88 emergency threshold. NO missing primitives.
calculators.realWorldPresence: NHS home-oximetry pathways, Cleveland Clinic and Mayo Clinic patient pages, smartwatch vendors' education pages; standalone interpreters are rare on reputable sites - differentiation opportunity.
calculators.cautions: Medically sensitive: the tool must instruct re-taking readings, must escalate conservatively (adopt the strictest labeled threshold when authorities differ), and must never reassure a symptomatic user (NHS: seek help if you feel more unwell regardless of the number). Note device accuracy limits (plus-or-minus 2-4%) and reduced accuracy on darker skin (may over-read). NHS thresholds originate from the COVID-19 home-monitoring pathway and WHO's from anaesthesia monitoring - state context on-screen. People with chronic lung disease may have a different personal target set by their clinician.

calculators.name: Six-Minute Walk Distance Reference (Enright & Sherrill)
calculators.whyRelevant: The 6MWT is the standard functional-capacity field test; a citable, closed-form reference equation exists (Enright & Sherrill 1998, verified via NCBI). Consumer-usable with a measured walk (e.g., smartwatch or track), so include - with protocol cautions.

inputs.label: Age
inputs.notes: Reference population was healthy adults aged 40-80.

calculators.logic: VERBATIM equations (Enright & Sherrill 1998, healthy adults 40-80y; PEFerence medians 576 m men / 494 m women): MEN: '6MWD = (7.57 x heightcm) - (5.02 x age) - (1.76 x weightkg) - 309 m'. WOMEN: '6MWD = (2.11 x heightcm) - (2.29 x weightkg) - (5.78 x age) + 667 m'. Percent predicted = measuredDistance / predicted6MWD * 100. The equations 'explained about 40% of the variance in the distance walked for healthy adults' and 'may be used to compute the percent predicted 6MWD for individual adult patients performing the test for the first time, when using the standardized protocol.' LOWER LIMIT OF NORMAL: subtraction constants exist in the full paper but were NOT verbatim-verifiable from trusted sources during this pass - DO NOT ship an LLN until verified (see openIssues).
calculators.outputScale: Predicted distance in meters (~300-800 m); optional % predicted.

resultCategories.label: At or above predicted
resultCategories.interpretation: Walking capacity at or above the average predicted for your age, sex, height and weight.
resultCategories.recommendation: Maintain regular physical activity; this reference explains only part of individual variation, so trends over time matter more than a single test.

resultCategories.label: Below predicted
resultCategories.interpretation: Walking capacity below the population-predicted average. The equations explain only ~40% of variance, so a below-average result is not by itself abnormal.
resultCategories.recommendation: If you also have breathlessness, fatigue, chest symptoms or a known heart/lung condition, discuss formal six-minute walk testing with your clinician; repeat under the same conditions to track change.

sources.title: Enright PL, Sherrill DL. Reference equations for the six-minute walk in healthy adults. Am J Respir Crit Care Med 1998;158(5 Pt 1):1384-7. PMID 9817683
6 Minute Walk Distance calculator (uses Enright & Sherrill)

calculators.platformMapping: condition DSL on sex; derived linear formula (multiplication/addition only); percent-predicted division; category bands. Unit conversions in->cm (2.54), lb->kg (0.45359237), ft->m (0.3048). NO missing primitives. LLN would be an additive adjustment once constants are verified.
calculators.realWorldPresence: MDCalc (6 Minute Walk Distance), QxMD, Medicalalgorithms.com, rehab/physio reference tools (Shirley Ryan AbilityLab).
calculators.cautions: The formal 6MWT uses a standardized supervised protocol (flat 30 m course, scripted encouragement); a casual self-timed walk under- or over-estimates. Applies only to ages 40-80 and healthy-population norms (derived from 117 men, 173 women in one US community); other cohorts differ substantially. Anyone with cardiac symptoms, recent MI or unstable angina should not self-test. Do not display an LLN until the subtraction constants are source-verified.

calculators.name: mMRC (Modified Medical Research Council) Breathlessness Scale
calculators.whyRelevant: One-question breathlessness grade used by GOLD for COPD symptom assessment; pairs naturally with the FEV1/FVC and pack-years tools. Tier 3: single select, low standalone SEO value, licensing nuance to resolve.

inputs.label: Which statement best describes your breathlessness?

options.label: I only get breathless with strenuous exercise
I get short of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill
On level ground, I walk slower than people of the same age because of breathlessness, or I have to stop for breath when walking at my own pace on the level
I stop for breath after walking about 100 yards or after a few minutes on level ground
I am too breathless to leave the house or I am breathless when dressing

inputs.notes: Statement wording verbatim from Launois et al., BMC Pulm Med 2012 (PMC3515513), Table 1.

calculators.logic: Score = selected grade (0-4). Grade texts verbatim (PMC3515513): Grade 0 'I only get breathless with strenuous exercise'; Grade 1 'I get short of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill'; Grade 2 'On level ground, I walk slower than people of the same age because of breathlessness, or I have to stop for breath when walking at my own pace on the level'; Grade 3 'I stop for breath after walking about 100 yards or after a few minutes on level ground'; Grade 4 'I am too breathless to leave the house or I am breathless when dressing'. StatPearls COPD chapter references the 'Modified Medical Research Council (mMRC) Dyspnea Scale (0 to 4)' as a standard COPD symptom measure.
calculators.outputScale: Grade 0-4 (higher = worse breathlessness)

resultCategories.label: Grade 0-1 (lower breathlessness burden)
resultCategories.interpretation: Breathlessness limited to strenuous exercise or hurrying/inclines - the lower-symptom stratum used in COPD assessment.
resultCategories.recommendation: If breathlessness is new, progressive, or out of proportion to activity, mention it to your clinician - especially if you smoke or smoked.

resultCategories.label: Grade 2-4 (higher breathlessness burden)
resultCategories.interpretation: Breathlessness that limits everyday walking or basic activities - the higher-symptom stratum in COPD assessment frameworks.
resultCategories.recommendation: Discuss with your clinician; combined with smoking history and spirometry this level of breathlessness typically warrants formal respiratory evaluation.

sources.title: Launois C et al. The modified Medical Research Council scale for the assessment of dyspnea in daily living in obesity. BMC Pulm Med 2012 (grade wording, Table 1)
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (mMRC 0-4 usage)

calculators.platformMapping: optionPoints (select maps directly to 0-4); category bands on the score (0-1 vs 2-4, higher-is-worse). NO missing primitives.
calculators.realWorldPresence: MDCalc (mMRC Dyspnea Scale), QxMD; embedded in GOLD ABE assessment tools; 'Calculated decisions: mMRC' published in evidence-based medicine practice literature (PMID 29068638).
calculators.cautions: The underlying MRC breathlessness scale originates with the UK Medical Research Council; it is very widely reproduced in open-access literature (the cited reproduction is CC-BY) but formal MRC permission terms should be confirmed before commercial deployment (see openIssues). The 2-4 vs 0-1 split reflects common COPD assessment practice; the specific GOLD >= 2 threshold should be cited to a GOLD/trusted source before displaying it as such.

calculators.name: Pregnancy Due Date Calculator (EDD)
calculators.whyRelevant: Highest-volume pregnancy query worldwide; natural companion to a wellness/lead-magnet funnel; every major health platform ships one.

inputs.label: How do you want to date the pregnancy?

options.label: First day of last menstrual period (LMP)
Ultrasound date + gestational age at scan

inputs.label: First day of last menstrual period
inputs.notes: Date picker. Required when datingMethod=lmp. Must be in the past, within ~44 weeks of today.

inputs.label: Average cycle length
inputs.notes: Default 28. Naegele assumes a 28-day cycle with ovulation on day 14 (StatPearls). Adjustment applied only for LMP method.

inputs.label: Conception date
inputs.notes: Required when datingMethod=conception.

inputs.label: IVF retrieval/transfer date
inputs.notes: Required for IVF methods.

inputs.label: Gestational age at ultrasound — extra days

calculators.logic: NAEGELE'S RULE (LMP method): EDD = LMP + 280 days. Equivalent procedure: 'Subtracts 3 months and adds 7 days to calculate the estimated due date (EDD)' (StatPearls NBK536986); 'Adding 7 days and then 9 months to the patient's last menstrual period (or 280 days) gives an estimated delivery date' (StatPearls NBK442018). Assumes 'a normal 28-day menstrual cycle and ovulates on day 14 of that cycle'. CYCLE-LENGTH ADJUSTMENT (Parikh's formula, StatPearls NBK536986): 'Adds nine months to the start of the last menstrual period, subtracting 21 days, then adding the duration of the previous cycle' — algebraically EDD = LMP + 280 + (cycleLength − 28) days. CONCEPTION METHOD: EDD = conception date + 266 days ('Fresh IVF: Add 266 days to egg retrieval/fertilization date', StatPearls NBK536986). IVF: day-3 frozen embryo transfer: EDD = transfer date + 263 days; day-5 blastocyst transfer: EDD = transfer date + 261 days (StatPearls NBK536986). ULTRASOUND METHOD: EDD = ultrasound date + (280 − GA-at-scan-in-days). ACOG CO 700 REDATING RULES (surface as informational panel): ultrasound before 9 0/7 weeks (i.e. ≤8 6/7 wks, CRL-based): redate if discrepancy from LMP dating is MORE THAN 5 DAYS; 9 0/7–13 6/7 weeks: more than 7 days; 14 0/7–15 6/7 weeks: more than 7 days; 16 0/7–21 6/7 weeks: more than 10 days; 22 0/7–27 6/7 weeks: more than 14 days; ≥28 0/7 weeks: ACOG Table 1 lists more than 21 days (StatPearls states third-trimester ultrasound accuracy '+/- 21 to 30 days'). Pregnancies without ultrasound confirmation of gestational age before 22 0/7 weeks are considered 'suboptimally dated'. When ART was used, the ART-derived EDD should be used (ACOG CO 700, search-verified). REVERSE (EDD method): LMP-equivalent = EDD − 280 days; current GA = 280 − (EDD − today) days.
calculators.outputScale: EDD calendar date; current gestational age (weeks + days); early/full/late/postterm window dates

resultCategories.label: Estimated due date
resultCategories.interpretation: The estimated date of delivery assumes a 280-day pregnancy from the first day of the LMP with ovulation at day 14.
resultCategories.recommendation: This is an estimate, not a promise of delivery day. ACOG advises first-trimester ultrasound as the most accurate dating method; discuss confirmation of your due date with your prenatal care provider, ideally before 22 0/7 weeks (paraphrased, ACOG CO 700 via StatPearls).

resultCategories.label: Early term window
resultCategories.interpretation: Delivery in this window is 'early term' per ACOG/SMFM CO 579.
resultCategories.recommendation: Outcomes are best at 39 weeks or later; avoid elective delivery before 39 weeks unless medically indicated (paraphrased ACOG CO 579).

resultCategories.label: Full term window
resultCategories.interpretation: 'Full term' per ACOG CO 579; best documented neonatal outcomes.
resultCategories.recommendation: Continue routine prenatal care; the EDD marks 40 0/7 weeks.

resultCategories.label: Late term
resultCategories.interpretation: 'Late term' per ACOG CO 579.
resultCategories.recommendation: Increased monitoring is typically discussed at this stage; follow your clinician's plan.

resultCategories.label: Postterm
resultCategories.interpretation: 'Postterm' per ACOG CO 579; MedlinePlus: infants born after 42 weeks are considered postmature.
resultCategories.recommendation: Clinical evaluation of continued pregnancy is standard; contact your prenatal provider.

calculators.name: Gestational Age Calculator
calculators.whyRelevant: Companion query to due date ('how many weeks pregnant am I'); same input set, distinct SEO page.
calculators.logic: DEFINITION (MedlinePlus 002367, verbatim): gestational age is 'measured in weeks, from the first day of the woman's last menstrual cycle to the current date.' CALCULATION: GA_days = asOfDate − LMP; display weeks = floor(GA_days/7), days = GA_days mod 7. From EDD: GA_days = 280 − (EDD − asOfDate). From ultrasound: GA_days = (usGaWeeks*7 + usGaDays) + (asOfDate − usDate). CLASSIFICATION: 'A normal pregnancy can range from 38 to 42 weeks gestation'; 'Infants born before 37 weeks are considered premature'; 'Infants born after 42 weeks are considered postmature' (MedlinePlus 002367 verbatim). ACOG CO 579 designations: early term 37 0/7–38 6/7; full term 39 0/7–40 6/7; late term 41 0/7–41 6/7; postterm ≥42 0/7 weeks.
calculators.outputScale: weeks + days (e.g. 24w 3d); classification band

resultCategories.recommendation: Continue routine prenatal visits.

resultCategories.label: Late term
resultCategories.interpretation: Late term per ACOG CO 579.
resultCategories.recommendation: Discuss monitoring/induction planning with your clinician.

resultCategories.label: Postterm
resultCategories.interpretation: Postterm (ACOG); postmature (MedlinePlus).
resultCategories.recommendation: Seek prompt obstetric evaluation.

inputs.label: Current gestational age

mergedFrom.logic: Cleveland Clinic (fetch-verified, verbatim): 'Pregnancy lasts about 40 weeks and is split into three trimesters that each last around 13 weeks.' 'The first trimester lasts until you're 13 weeks pregnant.' 'The second trimester consists of weeks 13 to 28.' 'The third trimester lasts from week 29 to 40.' calculators.name: Ovulation & Fertile Window Estimator
calculators.whyRelevant: Massive consumer search volume (ovulation calculator); pairs with menstrual-cycle and due-date tools for a conception-planning funnel.

inputs.label: First day of your last period
Average cycle length
inputs.notes: Default 28. Cleveland Clinic: 21–35 days normal for adults; ACOG CO 651: 21–45 days typical for adolescents.

inputs.label: Shortest cycle in last 6 months
inputs.notes: Only if irregular=true (calendar method).

inputs.label: Longest cycle in last 6 months
inputs.notes: Only if irregular=true. Must be >= shortestCycle.

calculators.logic: REGULAR-CYCLE ESTIMATE (luteal-phase rule): estimated ovulation = LMP + (cycleLength − 14) days. Basis: 'in an average menstrual cycle of 28 days, ovulation occurs about 14 days before the start of the next menstrual period' (ACOG Fertility Awareness FAQ, search-verified); NICHD (fetch-verified): 'Ovulation occurs at about day 14 of an average 28-day cycle'; NHS (fetch-verified): 'in most women it happens around 10 to 16 days before the next period'. Next period = LMP + cycleLength. FERTILE WINDOW: 6 days = day of ovulation plus the 5 days before it (ACOG FAQ: 'the fertile window only lasts 6 days each cycle—the day of ovulation, and the 5 days before it', search-verified). Cleveland Clinic (fetch-verified) alternative: about five days before ovulation through one day after — surface both, labeled by org. ACOG FAQ: fertile window typically Days 8–19 in cycles of 26–32 days (search-verified). GAMETE SURVIVAL (labeled by org): egg 'survives about 12 to 24 hours after ovulation' (Cleveland Clinic); 'a released egg lives for less than 24 hours' (MedlinePlus); sperm 'can live in your uterus for between three and five days' (Cleveland Clinic); 'less than 5 days' (MedlinePlus); 'up to 7 days after sex' (NHS). IRREGULAR CYCLES — CALENDAR METHOD (Cleveland Clinic, fetch-verified verbatim): 'Find your shortest cycle and your longest cycle in a six-month period. You subtract 18 days from your shortest cycle and 11 days from your longest cycle' → first fertile day = LMP + (shortestCycle − 18); last fertile day = LMP + (longestCycle − 11). MedlinePlus 007015: many couples plan intercourse between days 11 to 14 of a 28-day cycle; providers recommend sex between days 7 and 20; 'Having sex every other day or every third day works just as well as having sex every day.'
calculators.outputScale: estimated ovulation date; fertile window date range; next-period date

resultCategories.label: Estimated ovulation day
resultCategories.interpretation: Approximate day the ovary releases an egg; actual timing varies cycle to cycle (NHS: 10–16 days before the next period).
resultCategories.recommendation: If trying to conceive, intercourse every 1–3 days across the fertile window is as effective as daily (paraphrased MedlinePlus). Ovulation predictor kits (urine LH) help when cycles are irregular (MedlinePlus).

resultCategories.label: Fertile window
resultCategories.range: ovulation − 5 days through ovulation day (ACOG); Cleveland Clinic: through 1 day after
resultCategories.interpretation: Pregnancy is most likely from intercourse in the ~6 days ending on ovulation day, because sperm survive up to about 5 days while the egg survives less than 24 hours.
resultCategories.recommendation: Plan intercourse within this window when trying to conceive. This tool is NOT reliable as a stand-alone contraception method (conservative note consistent with ACOG fertility-awareness guidance).

resultCategories.label: Irregular-cycle fertile span (calendar method)
resultCategories.range: day (shortestCycle − 18) through day (longestCycle − 11) of the cycle
resultCategories.interpretation: Wider window reflecting cycle variability (Cleveland Clinic calendar method).
resultCategories.recommendation: Consider LH ovulation kits, basal body temperature, or cervical mucus tracking for more precision (Cleveland Clinic/MedlinePlus). See a clinician if cycles are <21 or >35 days apart or absent ≥90 days (Cleveland Clinic).

Ovulation FAQ 20458291

Regular/irregular branching = condition DSL on boolean. Fertile-window authority conflict (ACOG 6-day vs Cleveland +1 day) maps to the platform's labeled-conflict surfacing. No points/bands needed beyond validation.

calculators.name: Pregnancy Weight Gain Calculator (IOM/NAM 2009)
calculators.whyRelevant: Directly reuses the platform's BMI machinery; fully expressible in existing primitives TODAY (no date math needed); strong wellness-funnel fit.

inputs.label: Pre-pregnancy BMI
inputs.notes: BMI = weight_kg / (height_m)^2

calculators.logic: STEP 1 — BMI category (IOM 2009 / CDC-cited cutoffs, verbatim from CDC MMWR-linked material): underweight BMI <18.5; normal weight 18.5–24.9; overweight 25.0–29.9; obese ≥30.0. STEP 2 — SINGLETON total-gain recommendation (IOM/NAM 2009; lb per CDC, kg per IOM report as reproduced in PMC literature): underweight 28–40 lb (12.5–18 kg); normal weight 25–35 lb (11.5–16 kg); overweight 15–25 lb (7–11.5 kg); obese 11–20 lb (5–9 kg). RATES OF GAIN, 2nd and 3rd trimester (IOM 2009, kg/week, search-verified verbatim): underweight 0.44–0.58; normal 0.35–0.50; overweight 0.23–0.33; obese 0.17–0.27 kg/week. STEP 3 — TWINS (IOM 2009 provisional guidelines): normal weight 16.8–24.5 kg (37–54 lb); overweight 14.1–22.7 kg (31–50 lb); obese 11.3–19.1 kg (25–42 lb); ranges reflect the 25th–75th percentile of gain among women delivering twins ≥2500 g average at 37–42 weeks. Underweight + twins: IOM provides no recommendation (insufficient data) — output 'no established range; individualized clinical guidance needed'. STEP 4 (optional progress check, clearly labeled approximate): if currentWeight and gaWeeks given, gainToDate = currentWeight − prePregWeight; compare to band [rateLow*(gaWeeks−13), rateHigh*(gaWeeks−13)] + first-trimester allowance for gaWeeks>13 — first-trimester allowance value NOT verified this session (see openIssues); ship progress check only after verifying, or omit.
calculators.outputScale: recommended total gain range (kg and lb); weekly rate range; optional on-track/below/above flag

resultCategories.label: Below recommended range (progress check)
resultCategories.range: gain to date < lower bound for week
resultCategories.interpretation: Gaining less than the IOM range is associated with higher risk of small-for-gestational-age birth (paraphrased IOM 2009).
resultCategories.recommendation: Discuss nutrition with your prenatal provider; do not attempt restrictive dieting in pregnancy without clinical supervision.

resultCategories.label: Within recommended range
resultCategories.range: within IOM band for BMI category
resultCategories.interpretation: Weight gain consistent with IOM/NAM 2009 guidance for your pre-pregnancy BMI.
resultCategories.recommendation: Continue balanced nutrition and activity as advised by your prenatal provider.

resultCategories.label: Above recommended range
resultCategories.range: gain to date > upper bound for week
resultCategories.interpretation: Gain above the IOM range is associated with higher risk of large-for-gestational-age birth, cesarean delivery, and postpartum weight retention (paraphrased IOM 2009/CDC).
resultCategories.recommendation: Talk with your provider about diet and physical activity; never present weight-loss targets during pregnancy.

resultCategories.label: Twins — underweight BMI
resultCategories.interpretation: IOM 2009 found insufficient information to set a twin-gestation range for underweight women.
resultCategories.recommendation: Individualized guidance from the prenatal care team is required.

Committee Opinion No. 548: Weight Gain During Pregnancy

No new primitive required (dates avoided by asking week number directly).
calculators.realWorldPresence: CDC consumer guidance page; March of Dimes and What to Expect calculators; MSD Manual reference table; numerous OB clinic sites; Omni Calculator.
calculators.cautions: Never frame as weight-loss advice during pregnancy. Twin ranges are labeled 'provisional' by IOM — say so. lb/week display rates and first-trimester allowance need verification before launch (see openIssues). IOM data is public-domain US government-commissioned guidance; no licensing issues.

calculators.name: Menstrual Cycle Normality Checker
calculators.whyRelevant: Feeds the ovulation tool; 'is my cycle normal' is a common query; fully expressible in existing primitives.

inputs.label: Typical cycle length (day 1 of period to day 1 of next)
Severe pain, cramping, nausea or vomiting with periods?

calculators.logic: ADULTS (Cleveland Clinic, fetch-verified verbatim): 'A cycle can range in length from 21 days to about 35 days and still be normal' (average 28); 'Most people have their period (bleed) for between three and seven days'; day 1 = first day of bleeding. Abnormal flags (verbatim list): 'Periods that occur less than 21 days or more than 35 days apart'; 'Not having a period for three months (or 90 days)'; 'Period bleeding that lasts longer than seven days'; 'Bleeding or spotting that happens between periods'; 'Periods that are accompanied by severe pain, cramping, nausea or vomiting'. Concordant: NHS 'Regular cycles that are longer or shorter than this, from 21 to 35 days, are normal'; NICHD 'A normal menstrual cycle can vary between 21 and 35 days; 28 days is the average.' ADOLESCENTS (ACOG Committee Opinion 651, search-verified): normal menstrual cycle interval typically 21–45 days; menstrual flow length 7 days or less; 90% of adolescent cycles fall within 21–45 days. BAND LOGIC: adult normal cycle 21–35 d; adolescent normal cycle 21–45 d; normal bleeding ≤7 d (flag 3–7 d as typical for adults); daysSinceLastPeriod ≥90 → possible amenorrhea flag; any boolean red flag → 'discuss with clinician' output.
calculators.outputScale: per-parameter classification + overall 'typical / outside typical range' summary

resultCategories.label: Within typical range
resultCategories.range: cycle 21–35 d (adult) / 21–45 d (teen), bleeding ≤7 d, no red flags
resultCategories.interpretation: Cycle characteristics fall inside the ranges these authorities describe as normal.
resultCategories.recommendation: Track cycles; day 1 is the first day of bleeding. No action needed beyond routine care.

resultCategories.label: Cycle shorter than typical
resultCategories.interpretation: Cleveland Clinic lists periods occurring less than 21 days apart as an irregular pattern.
resultCategories.recommendation: Discuss with a clinician, especially if new or persistent (paraphrased Cleveland Clinic).

resultCategories.label: Cycle longer than typical
resultCategories.interpretation: Outside the normal interval per Cleveland Clinic (adults) / ACOG CO 651 (adolescents).
resultCategories.recommendation: Seek evaluation; ACOG treats the menstrual cycle as a 'vital sign' — persistent long cycles warrant review (paraphrased).

resultCategories.label: Prolonged bleeding
resultCategories.interpretation: Bleeding lasting longer than seven days is an abnormal pattern (Cleveland Clinic; ACOG flow norm ≤7 days).
resultCategories.recommendation: See a clinician to evaluate for causes including bleeding disorders (conservative paraphrase of ACOG adolescent guidance).

resultCategories.label: Possible amenorrhea
resultCategories.interpretation: 'Not having a period for three months (or 90 days)' is listed as abnormal (Cleveland Clinic).
resultCategories.recommendation: Take a pregnancy test if applicable and consult a clinician.

resultCategories.label: Red-flag symptoms
resultCategories.range: intermenstrual bleeding or severe pain/nausea/vomiting = yes
resultCategories.interpretation: Listed abnormal features (Cleveland Clinic).
resultCategories.recommendation: Medical evaluation recommended regardless of cycle length.

Committee Opinion No. 651: Menstruation in Girls and Adolescents: Using the Menstrual Cycle as a Vital Sign
sources.verification: search-verified (ACOG PDF located at acog.org media path; HTML page blocked)

Ovulation infographic (cycle 21–35 days, 28 average)

calculators.platformMapping: FULLY EXPRESSIBLE: numeric bands on cycleLength and bleedDays with age-group branching via condition DSL; boolean red flags via option points or condition branches; ≥90-day amenorrhea band on daysSinceLastPeriod. No new primitives.
calculators.realWorldPresence: Flo, Clue, Natural Cycles period trackers; Cleveland Clinic/NHS editorial content; no major standalone 'normality checker' — differentiation opportunity.
calculators.cautions: Screening/education only — must not output diagnoses (PCOS, thyroid etc.); direct red-flag results to clinicians. Adult vs adolescent ranges must stay separately labeled (ACOG vs Cleveland Clinic).

calculators.name: Pediatric Growth Percentile Calculator (WHO 0–2y / CDC 2–19y)
calculators.whyRelevant: Very high parent search demand and CDC/WHO ship reference calculators — but launch is blocked on multiple missing engine primitives; honest tier 2 (later catalog, after platform work).

inputs.label: Date of birth
inputs.notes: Age in months = (measurementDate − dob); needs date primitive. Alternative: direct age-in-months input.

calculators.logic: CHART SELECTION (CDC growth-chart training pages, search-verified): 'CDC recommends that health care providers use the World Health Organization (WHO) Child Growth Standard Charts for children birth to 2 years' and '2000 CDC Growth Charts for children and adolescents 2 years and older' (through age 19); switch at age 2. DATA: WHO Child Growth Standards (fetch-verified indicator list, who.int): length/height-for-age, weight-for-age, weight-for-length/height, BMI-for-age, head-circumference-for-age (plus arm circumference, skinfolds, velocity), ages 0–5 years; expanded tables with z-scores/percentiles downloadable per indicator (search-verified). CDC 2000 charts: percentile data files WITH LMS parameters downloadable (referenced page https://www.cdc.gov/growthcharts/percentile_data_files.htm): weight-for-age, length-for-age (birth–36 months), stature-for-age (2–20 y), BMI-for-age (2–20 y), head circumference (birth–36 months), weight-for-length/stature — each by sex and age with L (Box-Cox power), M (median), S (generalized coefficient of variation). COMPUTATION (CDC, search-verified verbatim): 'Z = [(X/M)^L – 1]/LS when L ≠ 0, or Z = ln(X/M)/S when L = 0'; percentile = standard normal CDF of Z ('a z-score of 1.96 is equal to the 97.5 percentile'). Age lookup requires row selection by sex + age-in-months and (for exact results) interpolation between half-month/month rows. BMI-for-age classification (CDC convention, NOT re-verified this session — cdc.gov blocked; see openIssues): underweight <5th percentile; healthy weight 5th–<85th; overweight 85th–<95th; obesity ≥95th percentile.
calculators.outputScale: percentile (and z-score) per measure; category band for BMI-for-age

resultCategories.label: Below 5th percentile (weight-for-age or BMI-for-age)
resultCategories.interpretation: Lower than 95% of reference children of the same age and sex.
resultCategories.recommendation: A single low measurement is not a diagnosis; growth TREND over time matters most. Review with the child's pediatrician (conservative, consistent with CDC training materials).

resultCategories.label: 5th to <85th percentile
resultCategories.interpretation: Within the range CDC labels healthy for BMI-for-age.
resultCategories.recommendation: Continue routine well-child monitoring.

resultCategories.label: 85th to <95th percentile (BMI-for-age)
resultCategories.interpretation: CDC overweight range for children 2–19 (pending re-verification).
resultCategories.recommendation: Discuss nutrition and activity with the pediatrician; do not apply adult BMI cutoffs to children.

resultCategories.label: ≥95th percentile (BMI-for-age)
resultCategories.interpretation: CDC obesity range for children 2–19 (pending re-verification).
resultCategories.recommendation: Pediatric evaluation recommended; interpretation always requires the clinical context and growth history.

sources.title: Child Growth Standards — Standards (indicators 0–5 years)
Computation of centiles and z-scores (growth reference computation PDF)
CDC Growth Charts percentile data files with LMS values
sources.verification: blocked-cited (existence and content search-verified via cdc.gov results)

sources.title: National Health Statistics Report 63: Construction of LMS Parameters for the CDC Growth Charts (Z formula)
Growth chart training — WHO standards birth to 2 years; CDC charts 2–19 years

calculators.platformMapping: REQUIRES FOUR NEW PRIMITIVES, flag before any build: (1) LOOKUP-DATASET primitive — bulk LMS tables (sex × age-in-months × {L,M,S}) for WHO 0–24m and CDC 24–240m charts, hundreds of rows per indicator, shipped as platform datasets (WHO expanded tables and CDC percentile data files are freely downloadable); (2) NORMAL CDF (z → percentile) — not expressible in the whitelisted math; (3) ln() — needed for the L=0 branch of the z formula (pow covers L≠0); (4) DATE ARITHMETIC + interpolation between adjacent age rows for exact age-in-months. Existing primitives cover: unit conversions, pow for (X/M)^L, category bands on the resulting percentile.
calculators.realWorldPresence: CDC BMI Percentile Calculator for Child and Teen; WHO Anthro / Anthro Survey Analyser software; PediTools (clinician-facing); embedded in every EHR pediatric module.
calculators.cautions: Data is public (WHO/CDC, no licensing). Do NOT approximate LMS with simplified curves — accuracy is the entire value. Single-point percentiles must carry 'trend matters more than one measurement' framing and pediatrician referral language. CDC BMI-for-age category cutoffs and the WHO-vs-CDC handoff at exactly 24 months need re-verification from cdc.gov before launch (site currently blocks automated fetch).

calculators.name: PHQ-9 Depression Severity (Patient Health Questionnaire-9)
calculators.whyRelevant: The most widely used depression screener in the world; self-administered, 9 items, public domain, instantly scoreable. Perfect fit for a wellness lead-magnet hub alongside Niro CWS, and the mental-health domain is currently absent from the catalog.

inputs.label: Little interest or pleasure in doing things
inputs.notes: Timeframe for ALL items: 'Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by any of the following problems?' (Kroenke 2001, verbatim).

inputs.label: Trouble falling or staying asleep, or sleeping too much
Feeling tired or having little energy
Feeling bad about yourself — or that you are a failure or have let yourself or your family down
Trouble concentrating on things, such as reading the newspaper or watching television
Moving or speaking so slowly that other people could have noticed? Or the opposite — being so fidgety or restless that you have been moving around a lot more than usual
Thoughts that you would be better off dead or of hurting yourself in some way
inputs.notes: SAFETY ITEM: any response > 0 must trigger the crisis-resources escalation regardless of total score (MDCalc: 'Perform suicide risk assessment in patients who respond positively to item 9').

inputs.label: Item-9 positive flag (internal)
inputs.notes: derived: q9_selfharm > 0 ? 1 : 0 — drives the crisis interstitial/category override.

calculators.logic: Total score = sum of items 1-9, each scored 0 (not at all), 1 (several days), 2 (more than half the days), 3 (nearly every day). Range 0-27. Verbatim from Kroenke 2001: 'The PHQ-9 is the depression module, which scores each of the 9 DSM-IV criteria as "0" (not at all) to "3" (nearly every day)' and 'PHQ-9 scores of 5, 10, 15, and 20 represented mild, moderate, moderately severe, and severe depression, respectively.' A score >=10 had sensitivity 88% and specificity 88% for major depression. Safety rule (independent of total): item 9 response > 0 triggers crisis-resource escalation. Note: the official instrument also contains a non-scored 10th functional-difficulty question ('how difficult have these problems made it for you...'), which does not enter the score.
calculators.outputScale: 0-27 total points (higher = more severe depressive symptoms)

resultCategories.label: Minimal or none
resultCategories.interpretation: Minimal or no depressive symptoms.
resultCategories.recommendation: No treatment indicated by score alone; monitor how you feel and re-screen if symptoms appear (per MDCalc interpretation of PHQ-9: 'Monitor; may not require treatment'). This is a screening score, not a diagnosis.

resultCategories.label: Mild
resultCategories.interpretation: Mild depressive symptoms (Kroenke 2001: score of 5 = mild).
resultCategories.recommendation: Consider discussing your mood with a healthcare professional, especially if symptoms persist or interfere with daily life; clinicians use judgment at this level (MDCalc: 'Use clinical judgment for treatment necessity').

resultCategories.label: Moderate
resultCategories.interpretation: Moderate depressive symptoms; a score >=10 had 88% sensitivity and 88% specificity for major depression in the validation study.
resultCategories.recommendation: Talk with a doctor or licensed mental-health professional — scores in this range generally warrant active evaluation and treatment discussion (MDCalc: 'Warrants active treatment').

resultCategories.label: Moderately severe
resultCategories.interpretation: Moderately severe depressive symptoms (Kroenke 2001: score of 15 = moderately severe).
resultCategories.recommendation: Seek professional evaluation promptly; treatment (psychotherapy and/or medication) is typically warranted at this level.

resultCategories.label: Severe
resultCategories.interpretation: Severe depressive symptoms (Kroenke 2001: score of 20 = severe).
resultCategories.recommendation: Seek professional care promptly. If you have any thoughts of self-harm, use the crisis resources immediately (call or text 988 in the US).

resultCategories.label: Safety escalation
resultCategories.interpretation: Positive response to the self-harm item requires safety follow-up regardless of total score.
resultCategories.recommendation: Show crisis interstitial verbatim resources (NIMH): 'In life-threatening situations, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.' 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: 'Call or text 988 or start a chat online to connect with a trained crisis counselor. The Lifeline provides 24-hour, confidential support to anyone in suicidal crisis or emotional distress.' Veterans: call 988 then press 1, or text 838255.

sources.org: Kroenke K, Spitzer RL, Williams JB — J Gen Intern Med (via PMC)
sources.title: The PHQ-9: Validity of a Brief Depression Severity Measure. J Gen Intern Med 2001;16(9):606-13. doi:10.1046/j.1525-1497.2001.016009606.x
PHQ-9 (Patient Health Questionnaire-9)

sources.org: PHQ Screeners (Pfizer) / instrument footer, corroborated by multiple PMC articles
sources.title: Public-domain status: 'Developed by Drs. Robert L. Spitzer, Janet B.W. Williams, Kurt Kroenke and colleagues, with an educational grant from Pfizer Inc. ... in the public domain. No permission required to reproduce, translate, display or distribute.'
Find Help — 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and emergency guidance

calculators.platformMapping: Fully expressible in existing primitives: 9 select inputs with optionPoints (0-3), additive aggregation to total, category bands 0-4/5-9/10-14/15-19/20-27 (higher-is-worse direction). Item-9 escalation = derived parameter `q9_flag = q9 > 0 ? 1 : 0` (whitelisted ternary) feeding an override category. MISSING (product-level, not math): a per-item alert/interstitial primitive so the crisis block renders prominently and BEFORE/alongside the score whenever q9_flag = 1 — if the engine can only render one category set per calculator, add a 'flagCategory override' or secondary-output primitive.
calculators.cautions: Screening tool, NOT a diagnostic instrument — results page must say a diagnosis requires a clinician. MUST display crisis resources (988 call/text/chat, 911 for emergencies) on the calculator page and escalate visually on any positive item-9 response. Public domain (no license needed) — keep the required footer attribution to Spitzer/Williams/Kroenke. Not validated as self-serve web triage for adolescents (PHQ-A is the teen adaptation); label as for adults 18+.
calculators.realWorldPresence: MDCalc, Medscape reference calculators, NHS/UK IAPT services, Mental Health America online screening, Apple Health 'Mental Wellbeing' feature (uses PHQ-9), virtually every EHR (Epic/Cerner) and telehealth intake flow.

calculators.name: GAD-7 Anxiety Severity (Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item)
calculators.whyRelevant: Companion instrument to PHQ-9 from the same public-domain family; the standard anxiety self-screen worldwide. Pairs naturally with PHQ-9 on one hub page and doubles SEO coverage of high-volume 'anxiety test' queries.

inputs.label: Feeling nervous, anxious, or on edge
inputs.notes: Timeframe for ALL items: over the past 2 weeks.

inputs.label: Not being able to stop or control worrying
Worrying too much about different things
Being so restless that it's hard to sit still
Feeling afraid as if something awful might happen

calculators.logic: Total = sum of 7 items, each 0 (not at all) / 1 (several days) / 2 (more than half the days) / 3 (nearly every day). Range 0-21. Severity bands (NCHS/NCBI Bookshelf NBK609621, verbatim): 'adults with scores of 0-4 are categorized as having none or minimal anxiety symptoms, while those with scores of 5-9, 10-14, or 15-21 are categorized as having mild, moderate, or severe anxiety symptoms, respectively.' Spitzer 2006 (primary paper): 'A cut point was identified that optimized sensitivity (89%) and specificity (82%)' — that cut point is 10 for probable GAD.
calculators.outputScale: 0-21 total points (higher = more severe anxiety symptoms)

resultCategories.label: Minimal
resultCategories.interpretation: None or minimal anxiety symptoms.
resultCategories.recommendation: No action indicated by the score; re-take if symptoms change. Screening score, not a diagnosis.

resultCategories.label: Mild
resultCategories.interpretation: Mild anxiety symptoms.
resultCategories.recommendation: Monitor; consider mentioning symptoms at your next healthcare visit, especially if they persist (MDCalc: 'Monitor').

resultCategories.label: Moderate
resultCategories.interpretation: Moderate anxiety symptoms; scores >=10 indicate a 'possible clinically significant condition' (MDCalc) — the Spitzer 2006 screening cut point.
resultCategories.recommendation: Discuss with a doctor or licensed mental-health professional for further assessment.

resultCategories.label: Severe
resultCategories.interpretation: Severe anxiety symptoms.
resultCategories.recommendation: Seek professional evaluation; 'active treatment probably warranted' (MDCalc). If anxiety includes thoughts of self-harm or crisis, call or text 988.

sources.org: Spitzer RL, Kroenke K, Williams JBW, Löwe B — Arch Intern Med (via PubMed)
sources.title: A brief measure for assessing generalized anxiety disorder: the GAD-7. Arch Intern Med 2006;166(10):1092-7. doi:10.1001/archinte.166.10.1092 (PMID 16717171)

sources.org: NCBI Bookshelf / National Health Statistics Reports (CDC-NCHS)
sources.title: Symptoms of Anxiety and Depression Among Adults: United States, 2019 and 2022 (GAD-7 band definitions 0-4/5-9/10-14/15-21)
GAD-7 (General Anxiety Disorder-7)
Public-domain status: 'No permission required to reproduce, translate, display or distribute' (developed with an educational grant from Pfizer Inc.)

calculators.platformMapping: Fully supported: 7 selects with optionPoints 0-3, additive sum, category bands 0-4/5-9/10-14/15-21, higher-is-worse. No new primitives. Reuse the same crisis-resources content block as PHQ-9 (static, not score-driven).
calculators.cautions: Screening tool, not diagnostic; also screens reasonably for panic/social anxiety/PTSD per literature but label it for generalized anxiety. Public domain — keep developer attribution footer. Display crisis-resources block (988) on the page as with all mental-health tools.
calculators.realWorldPresence: MDCalc, Medscape, NHS talking-therapies intake, Mental Health America screening, Apple Health Mental Wellbeing (uses GAD-7), standard in EHRs and telehealth.

calculators.name: Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10)
calculators.whyRelevant: The classic 10-item perceived-stress self-report (Cohen 1983); strong SEO topic ('stress test/score') and complements PHQ-9/GAD-7. Tier 2 rather than 1 because (a) no developer-published severity cutoffs exist and (b) commercial-use permission is unresolved.

inputs.label: In the last month, how often have you been upset because of something that happened unexpectedly?
inputs.notes: All items use timeframe 'in the last month' and 5-point scale 0=never, 1=almost never, 2=sometimes, 3=fairly often, 4=very often (verbatim scale labels from PMC5295754).

inputs.label: …felt that you were unable to control the important things in your life?
…felt confident about your ability to handle your personal problems? (REVERSE-SCORED)
inputs.notes: Reverse scoring implemented directly in option points: 0=very often … 4=never (verbatim mapping from PMC5295754).

inputs.label: …felt that things were going your way? (REVERSE-SCORED)
…found that you could not cope with all the things that you had to do?
…been able to control irritations in your life? (REVERSE-SCORED)
…felt that you were on top of things? (REVERSE-SCORED)
…been angered because of things that happened that were outside of your control?
…felt difficulties were piling up so high that you could not overcome them?

calculators.logic: Total = sum of 10 items after reverse-scoring the four positively stated items. Verbatim (Sandhu et al 2015, PMC5295754): responses on a '5-point Likert scale (0 = never, 1 = almost never, 2 = sometimes, 3 = fairly often, 4 = very often)'; 'Four positively stated items (item 4, 5, 7, and 8) are reversely scored (0 = very often, 1 = fairly often, 2 = sometimes, 3 = almost never, 4 = never)'. Total range 0-40; higher = more perceived stress. Timeframe: past month. IMPORTANT: the developer (Cohen) has published no clinical cutoffs; the widely circulated bands 0-13 low / 14-26 moderate / 27-40 high could NOT be verified from any allowlisted source and should be shown only as an unofficial convention with a caveat, or replaced by a continuous gradient display.
calculators.outputScale: 0-40 total points (higher = greater perceived stress); no validated clinical cutoffs

resultCategories.label: Lower perceived stress
resultCategories.interpretation: Your perceived-stress score is in the lower third of the possible range.
resultCategories.recommendation: Maintain current coping strategies (regular sleep, physical activity, social connection). Note on page: the PSS has no official diagnostic cutoffs; this banding is a common convention only.

resultCategories.label: Moderate perceived stress
resultCategories.interpretation: Mid-range perceived stress over the past month.
resultCategories.recommendation: Consider stress-management practices (activity, sleep hygiene, relaxation techniques) and talk to a professional if stress interferes with daily functioning.

resultCategories.label: High perceived stress
resultCategories.interpretation: Perceived stress is in the upper third of the range; chronic high stress is associated with adverse health outcomes.
resultCategories.recommendation: Consider speaking with a healthcare or mental-health professional; if distress feels unmanageable or includes thoughts of self-harm, call or text 988.

sources.org: Cohen S, Kamarck T, Mermelstein R — J Health Soc Behav (via PubMed)

calculators.name: Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS)
calculators.whyRelevant: The standard daytime-sleepiness screener (sleep apnea/narcolepsy funnel) and a high-volume search topic — but it is a COPYRIGHTED, LICENSED instrument. Documented here for completeness; DO NOT implement without a license. Tier 3 by instruction.

inputs.label: Sitting and reading
inputs.notes: The 8 situations listed here are descriptive paraphrases (per Cleveland Clinic's public explainer); the exact licensed wording must come from the licensed instrument.

inputs.label: Sitting inactive in a public place (e.g., a theater or a meeting)
As a passenger in a car for an hour without a break
Lying down to rest in the afternoon when circumstances permit
Sitting quietly after lunch without alcohol
In a car, while stopped for a few minutes in traffic

calculators.logic: Total = sum of 8 items, each rated 0-3 for likelihood of dozing. Verbatim (Rosenberg 2022, PMC9285450): 'for a total score of zero to 24, with higher scores indicating a greater severity of EDS. Scores of <=10 are commonly considered within the normal range, whereas scores of >10 indicate pathological EDS.' Also: 'changes of 2-3 points may be considered the minimum clinically important difference on the ESS.' Cleveland Clinic subdivision (verbatim ranges): 0-5 low daytime sleepiness (normal); 6-10 high daytime sleepiness (normal); 11-12 mild excessive daytime sleepiness; 13-15 moderate excessive daytime sleepiness; 16-24 severe excessive daytime sleepiness; 'If you score 11 or greater, you may need to change your sleeping habits at night' and see a provider for evaluation.
calculators.outputScale: 0-24 total points (higher = more daytime sleepiness); >10 = excessive daytime sleepiness

resultCategories.label: Low daytime sleepiness (normal)
resultCategories.interpretation: Within the normal range.
resultCategories.recommendation: No action needed based on this score.

resultCategories.label: High-normal daytime sleepiness
resultCategories.interpretation: Still within the commonly accepted normal range (<=10).
resultCategories.recommendation: If you feel your sleepiness affects daily activities, review sleep habits (duration, schedule).

resultCategories.label: Mild excessive daytime sleepiness
resultCategories.interpretation: Above the normal range; scores >10 indicate excessive daytime sleepiness.
resultCategories.recommendation: Consider improving nighttime sleep habits and discussing daytime sleepiness with a healthcare provider (Cleveland Clinic: a score of 11 or greater may warrant evaluation).

resultCategories.label: Moderate excessive daytime sleepiness
resultCategories.interpretation: Moderate pathological daytime sleepiness.
resultCategories.recommendation: See a healthcare provider — sleepiness at this level can signal a sleep disorder such as sleep apnea and may require sleep testing.

resultCategories.label: Severe excessive daytime sleepiness
resultCategories.interpretation: Severe daytime sleepiness, typical of significant sleep disorders (e.g., obstructive sleep apnea, narcolepsy).
resultCategories.recommendation: Seek medical evaluation promptly; avoid driving or operating machinery while drowsy.

sources.title: A new method for measuring daytime sleepiness: the Epworth sleepiness scale. Sleep 1991;14(6):540-5. doi:10.1093/sleep/14.6.540 (PMID 1798888) — original instrument

Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS): What It Is & Results (band subdivision 0-5/6-10/11-12/13-15/16-24)

calculators.cautions: COPYRIGHTED/LICENSED INSTRUMENT: copyright held by Murray Johns (1990-1997); reproduction without written consent is prohibited; a license is required for ALL use (fee payable for commercial users and IT companies), administered by Mapi Research Trust (eprovide.mapi-trust.org). Notably, MDCalc does not host the ESS — a strong signal of enforcement. If Niro wants a sleepiness tool without licensing, consider building a generic non-ESS sleep-habits questionnaire instead (do not imitate the 8 ESS items). Also: ESS is validated for adults; ESS-CHAD (children) is separately licensed.
calculators.realWorldPresence: Medscape reference calculator, hospital sleep-center intake forms (licensed), Cleveland Clinic explainer page; absent from MDCalc (licensing).

calculators.name: Recommended Sleep Duration by Age
calculators.whyRelevant: Zero-licensing, high-SEO ('how much sleep do I need'), directly consumer-appropriate, and feeds the lab-report/wellness lead-magnet narrative (sleep is a Niro CWS lifestyle domain). Pure lookup vs authoritative age bands.

inputs.label: Age
inputs.notes: Collect months for under-2s; months-to-years factor 1/12 = 0.0833333.

inputs.label: Usual sleep per 24 hours (including naps for young children)
Guideline set to compare against

options.label: AASM (American Academy of Sleep Medicine) — default

inputs.notes: Platform surfaces conflicts side-by-side; never merged.

calculators.logic: Look up the recommended range for the user's age, then classify usual_sleep_hours as below / within / above range. AASM pediatric consensus (Paruthi 2016, verbatim): infants 4-12 months '12 to 16 hours per 24 hours (including naps)'; children 1-2 years '11 to 14 hours per 24 hours (including naps)'; 3-5 years '10 to 13 hours per 24 hours (including naps)'; 6-12 years '9 to 12 hours per 24 hours'; teenagers 13-18 years '8 to 10 hours per 24 hours'. AASM makes NO recommendation for infants <4 months. AASM/SRS adult consensus (Watson 2015, verbatim): 'Adults should sleep 7 or more hours per night on a regular basis to promote optimal health' (applies to ages 18-60); 'Sleeping less than 7 hours per night on a regular basis is associated with adverse health outcomes, including weight gain and obesity, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease and stroke, depression, and increased risk of death'; 'Sleeping more than 9 hours per night on a regular basis may be appropriate for young adults, individuals recovering from sleep debt, and individuals with illnesses. For others, it is uncertain whether sleeping more than 9 hours per night is associated with health risk.' National Sleep Foundation (Hirshkowitz 2015, search-verified): newborns 14-17 h; infants 12-15 h; toddlers 11-14 h; preschoolers 10-13 h; school-aged 9-11 h; teenagers 8-10 h; young adults and adults 7-9 h; older adults 7-8 h. WHO under-5 (for cross-reference, fetch-verified): 0-3 months 14-17 h; 4-11 months 12-16 h; 1-2 years 11-14 h; 3-4 years 10-13 h (quality sleep including naps).
calculators.outputScale: Classification: below / within / above the age-specific recommended range (hours per 24h)

resultCategories.label: Below recommended range
resultCategories.interpretation: You are getting less sleep than the amount recommended for your age group on a regular basis; in adults this is associated with weight gain and obesity, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease and stroke, depression, and increased risk of death (AASM/SRS).
resultCategories.recommendation: Aim to extend sleep toward the recommended range (consistent schedule, earlier bedtime, limiting evening screens/caffeine). Persistent inability to sleep enough, or loud snoring/gasping, merits discussion with a healthcare provider.

resultCategories.label: Within recommended range
resultCategories.interpretation: Your usual sleep duration matches the consensus recommendation for your age group.
resultCategories.recommendation: Keep a regular sleep schedule; duration is only one dimension — poor sleep quality or daytime sleepiness despite adequate hours still warrants attention.

resultCategories.label: Above recommended range
resultCategories.interpretation: AASM/SRS: sleeping more than 9 hours per night may be appropriate for young adults, people recovering from sleep debt, and people with illnesses; for others it is uncertain whether it carries health risk.
resultCategories.recommendation: If long sleep is new, unrefreshing, or accompanied by daytime fatigue, mention it to a healthcare provider.

resultCategories.label: No recommendation (AASM)
resultCategories.interpretation: AASM issues no sleep-duration recommendation for infants under 4 months (insufficient evidence and wide normal variation). NSF lists 14-17 h for newborns (0-3 months) — shown labeled as NSF.
resultCategories.recommendation: Discuss infant sleep patterns with your pediatrician.

sources.org: AASM — Paruthi S et al, J Clin Sleep Med (via PMC)
sources.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine. J Clin Sleep Med 2016;12(6):785-786

sources.org: AASM/SRS — Watson NF et al, Sleep (via PMC)
sources.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult: A Joint Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society. Sleep 2015;38(6):843-844. doi:10.5665/sleep.4716
