sources.title: National Sleep Foundation's sleep time duration recommendations: methodology and results summary. Sleep Health 2015;1(1):40-43
To grow up healthy, children need to sit less and play more (guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 — includes sleep amounts)

calculators.platformMapping: Existing primitives suffice: condition DSL branches on age (months/years) select the band table; numeric band scoring with min-inclusive/exclusive edges classifies usual_sleep_hours as below/within/above; unit conversion months->years via existing factors. The AASM-vs-NSF toggle = context branch in the condition DSL. No new primitives. (If the platform wants both authorities rendered simultaneously, that is the existing 'surface conflicts' display pattern, not an engine change.)
calculators.cautions: Recommendations apply to healthy individuals without sleep disorders (NSF explicitly limits to 'healthy individuals... not suffering from a sleep disorder'). AASM has no <4-month recommendation. Adult AASM statement formally covers ages 18-60; for 61+ show NSF older-adult 7-8 h labeled as NSF. CDC's consumer sleep page (which mirrors AASM) returned HTTP 403 during this pass — primary consensus statements used instead.
calculators.realWorldPresence: CDC 'About Sleep' page (AASM table), Mayo Clinic 'How many hours of sleep do you need', NHLBI sleep education pages, countless consumer calculators.

calculators.name: Daily Caffeine Intake Calculator
calculators.whyRelevant: Simple additive tool with strong FDA anchor (400 mg/day) and a pregnancy branch (ACOG 200 mg/day); consumer-appropriate, licensing-free, good wellness lead-magnet fit. Tier 2 because per-beverage content values vary between authorities and by product.

inputs.label: Coffee (8-oz cups)
inputs.notes: FDA: an 8-oz cup of coffee contains 'closer to 80 to 100 milligrams' — use 90 mg midpoint as the factor, surfaced to the user. MedlinePlus lists 95-200 mg (conflict recorded).

inputs.label: Green or black tea (8-oz cups)
inputs.notes: FDA: 8 oz of green or black tea contains '30-50 milligrams' — use 40 mg midpoint. MedlinePlus: tea 14-60 mg (conflict recorded).

inputs.label: Caffeinated soft drink (12-oz cans)
inputs.notes: FDA: a 12-oz can 'typically contains 30 to 40 milligrams' — use 35 mg midpoint. MedlinePlus: cola 35-45 mg per 12 oz.

inputs.label: Energy drink (8-oz servings)
inputs.notes: FDA: 'Caffeine in energy drinks can range from 40-250 mg per 8 fluid ounces' — too wide for a single factor; default 145 mg midpoint with a strong 'check the label' prompt. MedlinePlus: 70-100 mg per 8 oz (conflict recorded).

inputs.label: Other caffeine (label-read, e.g. espresso drinks, supplements, chocolate)
Pregnant, trying to conceive, or breastfeeding?
inputs.notes: Switches the comparison threshold from FDA 400 mg to ACOG <200 mg.

calculators.logic: total_mg = coffee_8oz_cups*90 + tea_8oz_cups*40 + soda_12oz_cans*35 + energy_drink_8oz*145 + other_caffeine_mg (per-beverage midpoints derived from FDA ranges; display the FDA ranges verbatim next to each input: coffee 8 oz = 80-100 mg; green/black tea 8 oz = 30-50 mg; caffeinated soft drink 12 oz = 30-40 mg; energy drink 8 oz = 40-250 mg). Threshold logic: if pregnancy_context then limit = 200 mg (ACOG: 'Moderate caffeine consumption (less than 200 mg per day) does not appear to be a major contributing factor in miscarriage or preterm birth'), else limit = 400 mg (FDA: 'For healthy adults, FDA has cited 400 milligrams a day — that's about four or five cups of coffee — as an amount not generally associated with dangerous, negative effects'). FDA also notes wide variation in sensitivity and metabolism, and that some conditions and medications increase sensitivity.
calculators.outputScale: Estimated total mg caffeine/day vs applicable limit (400 mg adult / 200 mg pregnancy)

resultCategories.label: Within cited limit
resultCategories.interpretation: Estimated intake is below the FDA-cited 400 mg/day for healthy adults (or the ACOG <200 mg/day level in pregnancy).
resultCategories.recommendation: Caffeine sensitivity varies widely between people; if you notice restlessness, insomnia, headaches, fast heart rate, or anxiety (MedlinePlus symptom list), consider cutting back regardless of the number.

resultCategories.label: Above cited limit
resultCategories.interpretation: Estimated intake meets or exceeds 400 mg/day, the amount FDA cites as 'not generally associated with dangerous, negative effects' for healthy adults — amounts above this are less well characterized.
resultCategories.recommendation: Consider reducing intake gradually (abrupt stopping can cause withdrawal headaches). People with sleep disorders, migraines, anxiety, GERD, ulcers, arrhythmia, high blood pressure — or who take interacting medications — should discuss caffeine with a healthcare provider (MedlinePlus).

resultCategories.label: Above pregnancy guidance
resultCategories.interpretation: ACOG advises that moderate caffeine consumption means less than 200 mg per day (about the amount in two cups of moderate-strength coffee); below that level it does not appear to be a major contributing factor in miscarriage or preterm birth.
resultCategories.recommendation: Reduce intake to under 200 mg/day and discuss caffeine with your obstetric provider; caffeine passes through the placenta (MedlinePlus).

sources.title: Spilling the Beans: How Much Caffeine is Too Much? (400 mg/day; per-beverage contents) — canonical page returned 404/403 during this pass; values confirmed verbatim from fda.gov-indexed search results
Committee Opinion No. 462: Moderate Caffeine Consumption During Pregnancy. Obstet Gynecol 2010;116:467-8 (<200 mg/day)
Caffeine (400 mg safe for most adults; per-beverage contents: coffee 8 oz 95-200 mg, tea 8 oz 14-60 mg, cola 12 oz 35-45 mg, energy drink 8 oz 70-100 mg; who should limit; overdose symptoms)

calculators.platformMapping: Existing primitives suffice: derived parameter with weighted sum (whitelisted + and *), condition DSL branch on pregnancy_context for the threshold, category bands on total_mg with direction higher-is-worse, unit conversion factors for mL->cups. Per-beverage mg factors live in config as adjustable constants. No new primitives. The FDA-vs-MedlinePlus content-range conflict uses the platform's existing conflict-surfacing display.
calculators.cautions: Estimates only — actual caffeine content varies by brand/brew strength (energy drinks span 40-250 mg per 8 oz per FDA); always prompt label checks. Do not present 400 mg as a 'safe line' — FDA frames it as 'not generally associated with dangerous, negative effects' with wide individual variation. Children/adolescents: no verified allowlisted threshold found — do not display a pediatric limit (open issue). Pure/highly-concentrated caffeine products are dangerous (FDA warns a teaspoon of powdered caffeine ~3,200 mg, about 2.5x a toxic dose) — worth a static warning line.
calculators.realWorldPresence: Mayo Clinic and Cleveland Clinic caffeine content articles, MedlinePlus, numerous consumer caffeine calculators (caffeineinformer etc.); no licensing barriers.

calculators.name: WHO Physical Activity Target Checker
calculators.whyRelevant: Activity is a core wellness-score domain; WHO 2020 guidelines give clean, quotable weekly targets by age group. Free to implement, complements the sleep and caffeine tools in a lifestyle cluster.

inputs.label: Weekly moderate-equivalent minutes (internal)
inputs.notes: derived: moderate_min_week + 2 * vigorous_min_week (WHO equivalence implied by 150-300 moderate vs 75-150 vigorous).

calculators.logic: WHO 2020 guideline targets (verbatim via NCBI Bookshelf mirror NBK566046): Adults 18-64 — 'at least 150-300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity; or at least 75-150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic physical activity' per week plus 'muscle-strengthening activities at moderate or greater intensity that involve all major muscle groups on 2 or more days a week'. Older adults 65+ — same aerobic and strength targets plus 'varied multicomponent physical activity that emphasizes functional balance and strength training at moderate or greater intensity, on 3 or more days a week'. Children/adolescents 5-17 — 'at least an average of 60 minutes per day of moderate- to vigorous-intensity, mostly aerobic, physical activity, across the week' and 'Vigorous-intensity aerobic activities, as well as those that strengthen muscle and bone, should be incorporated at least 3 days a week'; 'limit the amount of time spent being sedentary, particularly the amount of recreational screen time'. Pregnant/postpartum — 'at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic physical activity throughout the week' with 'a variety of aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities'. Adult classification: aerobic_equivalent = moderate + 2*vigorous; <150 = below target; 150-299 = meets minimum; >=300 = meets upper/optimal range. Strength met if strength_days_week >= 2; (65+) balance met if balance_days_week >= 3. Child classification: mvpa_daily_min >= 60 average = meets.
calculators.outputScale: Per-component classification (aerobic / strength / balance) against WHO weekly targets; adult aerobic expressed in moderate-equivalent minutes

resultCategories.label: Below aerobic target
resultCategories.interpretation: Below WHO's minimum of 150-300 minutes moderate (or 75-150 vigorous) weekly.
resultCategories.recommendation: Any amount helps — WHO notes replacing sedentary time with activity of any intensity provides health benefits; build gradually toward 150 minutes/week.

resultCategories.label: Meets minimum aerobic target
resultCategories.interpretation: Within WHO's recommended 150-300 moderate-equivalent minutes per week.
resultCategories.recommendation: For additional health benefits, progress toward the upper end (300 moderate-equivalent minutes) and keep 2+ strength days weekly.

resultCategories.label: Meets full aerobic range
resultCategories.interpretation: At or above the top of WHO's recommended range.
resultCategories.recommendation: Maintain; ensure muscle-strengthening 2+ days/week (and, if 65+, balance/functional training 3+ days/week to help prevent falls).

resultCategories.label: Below youth target
resultCategories.interpretation: Below WHO's 'at least an average of 60 minutes per day of moderate- to vigorous-intensity' activity.
resultCategories.recommendation: Increase active play/sport toward a 60-minute daily average, include vigorous and muscle/bone-strengthening activity at least 3 days a week, and limit recreational screen time.

resultCategories.label: Strength component not met
resultCategories.interpretation: WHO recommends muscle-strengthening for all major muscle groups on 2 or more days a week (adults and older adults).
resultCategories.recommendation: Add two nonconsecutive resistance-training days covering all major muscle groups.

sources.title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour — Recommendations (NBK566046)
Physical activity fact sheet (sedentary behaviour definition; all age groups should limit sedentary time)

sources.org: Bull FC et al — Br J Sports Med (via PMC)
sources.title: World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (PMC7719906) — corroborates 150-300/75-150 and 2+ strength days

calculators.platformMapping: Existing primitives suffice: derived formula aerobic_equivalent = moderate + 2*vigorous (whitelisted + and *); condition DSL branch on age_group/pregnancy context; numeric bands at 150/300 thresholds (higher-is-better direction); separate boolean-style bands for strength (>=2 days) and balance (>=3 days). Multi-component result = existing weighted-domains/multiple-category output pattern. No new primitives.
calculators.cautions: General population guidance — people with chronic conditions or disability have separate WHO recommendations (not modeled here); advise medical clearance if currently inactive with cardiovascular risk. The 2x vigorous-to-moderate equivalence is a standard WHO/HHS convention but state it on-page. Pregnancy branch should carry a 'confirm with your obstetric provider' line.
calculators.realWorldPresence: CDC/HHS activity guideline pages, NHS Live Well activity guidance, Mayo Clinic exercise articles; activity-target rings in consumer wearables reflect the same 150-min construct.

calculators.name: Child Screen Time Checker (WHO / AAP)
calculators.whyRelevant: Parent-facing lifestyle tool with clean WHO under-5 limits and AAP guidance to 5+; niche relative to the flagship wellness tools and inherently two-authority (WHO vs AAP), so tiered 3 (optional catalog filler).

inputs.label: Average recreational (sedentary) screen time per day
inputs.notes: Exclude video chatting with family (AAP exception).

calculators.logic: Age-branched comparison, both authorities shown labeled. WHO (fetch-verified, under-5 guidelines): infants <1 year — screen time 'not recommended'; 1-year-olds — sedentary screen time 'not recommended'; 2-year-olds — 'maximum 1 hour' (less is better); 3-4 years — 'maximum 1 hour daily (less is preferable)'. AAP via healthychildren.org (search-verified): 'screen time be avoided from birth to 18 months (except for video chatting with loved ones)'; 18-24 months — parents who want to introduce digital media 'should choose high-quality programming/apps and co-watch limited amounts together'; 2-5 years — 'limited to 1 hour or less per day of high-quality programming'; 6+ — set consistent limits so media does not displace sleep and physical activity (no fixed hour cap). Classification: for age < 12 months: any screen time > 0 = above guidance (both orgs); 12-24 months: WHO(1y) none recommended vs AAP(18-24mo) limited co-viewed high-quality — show both; 24-60 months: > 1 hour/day = above guidance (both orgs align at <=1 h); >= 72 months: no numeric cap — qualitative guidance only.
calculators.outputScale: Within / above age-specific guidance, per authority (WHO under-5; AAP through childhood)

resultCategories.label: Above guidance (WHO & AAP)
resultCategories.interpretation: WHO: screen time is not recommended under 1 year. AAP: avoid screens from birth to 18 months except video chatting.
resultCategories.recommendation: Replace screen exposure with interactive floor play, reading, and (WHO) at least 30 minutes of tummy time daily for infants; video chatting with loved ones is the accepted exception.

resultCategories.label: Authority-dependent
resultCategories.interpretation: WHO: sedentary screen time not recommended for 1-year-olds; maximum 1 hour for 2-year-olds. AAP: from 18-24 months, only high-quality programming co-viewed with a parent, in limited amounts.
resultCategories.recommendation: If introducing media at 18-24 months, choose high-quality content and always watch together; keep it minimal.

resultCategories.label: Above guidance (WHO & AAP)
resultCategories.interpretation: WHO (2-4 y): no more than 1 hour of sedentary screen time daily, less is better. AAP (2-5 y): limit to 1 hour or less per day of high-quality programming.
resultCategories.recommendation: Trim toward <=1 hour of high-quality, co-viewed content; protect sleep, physical play, and reading time.

resultCategories.label: Within guidance
resultCategories.interpretation: Within both WHO and AAP limits for this age.
resultCategories.recommendation: Favor high-quality programming and co-viewing; keep bedtimes and mealtimes screen-free.

resultCategories.label: No numeric cap — qualitative guidance
resultCategories.interpretation: AAP sets no fixed hour limit for 6+; the emphasis is consistent limits that do not displace sleep, physical activity, and other healthy behaviors.
resultCategories.recommendation: Use a family media plan: consistent daily limits, media-free bedrooms/bedtime, and ensure WHO's 60-minute daily activity target and age-appropriate sleep are met first.

sources.title: To grow up healthy, children need to sit less and play more — guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years of age

Where We Stand: Screen Time / healthy digital media use habits (avoid birth-18 months except video chat; 18-24 months co-viewed high-quality; 2-5 years <=1 hour/day) — canonical page URL returned 404 this pass; statements confirmed from healthychildren.org-indexed results

calculators.platformMapping: Existing primitives suffice: condition DSL on age (months), bands on recreational_screen_hours_day per branch (lower-is-better direction), months/years unit conversion. Dual-authority output uses the existing conflict-surfacing pattern (WHO vs AAP labels). No new primitives.
calculators.cautions: WHO limits apply to sedentary recreational screen time (schoolwork excluded); AAP explicitly exempts video chatting. WHO under-5 guidance ends at age 4; AAP is the only authority modeled for 5+. Guidance, not a medical score — frame results as parenting guidance, no diagnosis.
calculators.realWorldPresence: AAP Family Media Plan tool (healthychildren.org), WHO press materials, pediatric clinic handouts; few calculator-style implementations — modest differentiation opportunity.

calculators.name: Transferrin Saturation (TSAT) Calculator
calculators.whyRelevant: Iron studies are among the most common follow-ups to the platform's existing ferritin biomarker; TSAT is the standard derived value that makes serum iron + TIBC interpretable for iron deficiency and iron overload screening in a wellness/lab-report lead magnet.

inputs.label: Sex
inputs.notes: Drives sex-specific normal band (MedlinePlus)

calculators.logic: TSAT (%) = (serumIron / TIBC) x 100. Source verbatim (StatPearls NBK559119): "Percentage transferrin saturation is calculated by dividing serum iron by TIBC and multiplying the result by 100." Both inputs must be in the same unit before dividing (ratio is unit-invariant if consistent). Guard: TIBC > 0; also flag if serumIron > TIBC (implausible, entry error).

resultCategories.label: Suggestive of iron-deficient state
resultCategories.interpretation: StatPearls: "The total transferrin saturation falls to 16% or less during iron-deficient states."
resultCategories.recommendation: A low saturation, especially with low ferritin, can point to iron deficiency. Share these results with your healthcare provider before taking iron supplements — do not self-treat.

resultCategories.label: Below sex-specific normal
resultCategories.interpretation: Below the MedlinePlus normal band for your sex (Males: 20% to 50%; Females: 15% to 45%) but above the 16% deficiency marker where applicable.
resultCategories.recommendation: Borderline-low values are common and lab-dependent; discuss with your provider, particularly if you have fatigue or a low ferritin.

resultCategories.label: Normal
resultCategories.range: male 20-50%, female 15-45% (MedlinePlus); StatPearls narrower optimal 25-35% shown as secondary note
resultCategories.interpretation: Saturation within the reference band for your sex.
resultCategories.recommendation: No action needed based on this value alone.

resultCategories.label: Above sex-specific normal
resultCategories.interpretation: Higher than the MedlinePlus reference band. Persistently high saturation can be associated with iron overload states.
resultCategories.recommendation: An isolated high value does not diagnose anything; your provider may repeat fasting iron studies and review ferritin before considering causes such as hereditary hemochromatosis.

sources.title: Iron-Binding Capacity
Serum iron test

calculators.platformMapping: derived parameter: tsat = serumIron / tibc * 100 (whitelisted / and *); unit conversion factors on both inputs; condition DSL sex branch selects band set; category bands with min-inclusive edge control (≤16 vs <20). No missing primitives. Implausible-input flag (serumIron > tibc) maps to a derived boolean via ternary + a floor/validation rule.
calculators.realWorldPresence: Reported on every commercial iron panel (Quest, Labcorp); MDCalc and lab-interpretation tools compute it; standard in hemochromatosis screening pathways.
calculators.cautions: Serum iron has strong diurnal variation and is affected by recent meals/supplements — recommend fasting morning draw in copy. Conflicting normal bands (MedlinePlus sex-specific vs StatPearls 25-35%) must be surfaced per org, not merged. Educational disclaimer required; not a diagnosis.

calculators.name: Albumin-Corrected Calcium Calculator
calculators.whyRelevant: Total calcium is on virtually every metabolic panel and albumin is already one of the platform's 40 biomarkers; correction is the single most common derived chemistry value users encounter on lab reports.
calculators.logic: Corrected calcium (mg/dL) = totalCalcium + 0.8 x (4 - albumin), with albumin in g/dL. Source verbatim (StatPearls NBK430912): "Total serum calcium should be corrected by adding approximately 0.8 mg/dL for each 1 g/dL decrease in serum albumin below 4 gm/dL" (equivalently "Total calcium decreases by approximately 0.8 mg/dL (0.25 mmol/L) for every 1 g/dL (10 g/L) reduction in the serum albumin below the reference value of 4 g/dL"). MDCalc concurs on normal albumin = "4 g/dL or 40 g/L". Apply correction only when albumin < 4 g/dL (do not correct downward for high albumin in consumer context).
calculators.outputScale: mg/dL (also displayable as mmol/L x 0.2495)

resultCategories.label: Low (possible hypocalcemia)

resultCategories.interpretation: StatPearls: normal total serum calcium is "8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL (2.12-2.62 mmol/L)"; "Values below this range indicate hypocalcemia." MedlinePlus normal: "8.8 to 10.3 mg/dL (2.20 and 2.58 mmol/L)".
resultCategories.recommendation: A low corrected value should be confirmed by your provider — often with an ionized calcium test — before any conclusion is drawn.

resultCategories.label: Normal
resultCategories.interpretation: Corrected calcium in the reference range; an apparently low total calcium was likely explained by low albumin.
resultCategories.recommendation: No action needed based on this value alone.

resultCategories.label: High
resultCategories.interpretation: Above the reference range (possible hypercalcemia).
resultCategories.recommendation: Discuss with your provider; repeat testing and ionized calcium are typical next steps.

calculators.name: LDL Cholesterol (Friedewald) Calculator
calculators.whyRelevant: Lets users with only TC/HDL/TG (common on basic panels) estimate LDL, non-HDL, and VLDL — directly feeds the existing lipid biomarkers and heart-risk calculator; strong SEO head-term.

inputs.label: Triglycerides (fasting)
inputs.notes: Hard validity gate at 400 mg/dL — refuse calculation at or above

calculators.logic: Convert all inputs to mg/dL first, then: LDL-C = totalCholesterol - hdl - triglycerides/5 (StatPearls NBK542294 verbatim: "LDL-C = (Total cholesterol) − (HDL-C) − (Triglycerides/5), in milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL)"). Secondary outputs: non-HDL = totalCholesterol - hdl; VLDL ≈ triglycerides/5. VALIDITY: formula "inaccurate in patients with hypertriglyceridemia (up to 4.5 mmol/L or 400 mg/dL)" (StatPearls) and MDCalc: "known to be inaccurate at extremely high triglyceride (>400 mg/dL) and total cholesterol levels" — block output when TG ≥ 400 mg/dL and show a see-your-lab message. Also require fasting sample in copy. LDL bands (StatPearls, ATP III): Optimal <100; Near optimal/above optimal 100-129; Borderline high 130-159; High 160-189; Very high >190 mg/dL.
calculators.outputScale: mg/dL (LDL typically 0-300)

resultCategories.label: Optimal
resultCategories.interpretation: ATP III (via StatPearls): Optimal.
resultCategories.recommendation: Maintain heart-healthy habits; recheck per your provider's schedule.

resultCategories.label: Near optimal / above optimal
resultCategories.interpretation: ATP III: Near optimal/above optimal.
resultCategories.recommendation: Lifestyle measures (diet, activity) are the usual first step; discuss your overall cardiovascular risk with your provider.

resultCategories.label: Borderline high
resultCategories.interpretation: ATP III: Borderline high.
resultCategories.recommendation: Worth reviewing with your provider alongside your full risk profile (the platform's heart-risk calculator can help frame this).

resultCategories.label: High
resultCategories.interpretation: ATP III: High.
resultCategories.recommendation: See your provider to discuss risk-reduction options; do not start or change medication on your own.

resultCategories.label: Very high
resultCategories.interpretation: ATP III: Very high.
resultCategories.recommendation: Discuss promptly with your provider; very high LDL sometimes reflects familial hypercholesterolemia.

resultCategories.label: Not calculable
resultCategories.interpretation: The Friedewald equation is unreliable at this triglyceride level.
resultCategories.recommendation: Ask your lab/provider for a direct LDL measurement.

calculators.name: Neutrophil-to-Lymphocyte Ratio (NLR) Calculator
calculators.whyRelevant: Popular wellness/longevity metric computable from the CBC differential the platform now covers; must be framed cautiously because interpretation is not clinically standardized.
calculators.logic: NLR = anc / alc (dimensionless). Normal range in healthy non-geriatric adults (Forget et al. 2017, BMC Res Notes, PMC5217256, n=413 workers age 21-66): "The mean NLR is 1.65 [±1.96 SD: 0.78–3.53]"; conclusion verbatim: "normal NLR values in an adult, non-geriatric, population in good health are between 0.78 and 3.53." No standardized disease cutoffs — do not band beyond normal/outside-normal.
calculators.outputScale: ratio, typically 0.5-10

resultCategories.label: Within the healthy-adult reference range
resultCategories.interpretation: Within the range observed in healthy non-geriatric adults (Forget 2017).
resultCategories.recommendation: No action needed based on this ratio alone.

resultCategories.label: Outside the healthy-adult reference range
resultCategories.interpretation: Outside the healthy-adult study range. NLR rises with acute infection, inflammation, physiologic stress, and steroid use; interpretation thresholds are not standardized, and the reference range was derived from adults aged 21-66 (authors caution "age is certainly a limit").
resultCategories.recommendation: An out-of-range ratio is a nonspecific finding, not a diagnosis. If your CBC was otherwise normal and you feel well, it may mean little; review the underlying neutrophil and lymphocyte counts with your provider.

sources.title: Forget P, et al. What is the normal value of the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio?

calculators.platformMapping: derived parameter anc / alc; two bands. No missing primitives. If users only have percentages + total WBC, add derived params anc = wbc * neutPct / 100 (pure arithmetic, supported).
calculators.realWorldPresence: Widely computed in longevity/biohacking communities and research literature; MDCalc hosts NLR-adjacent scores; not a standard clinical panel item.
calculators.cautions: Research-grade metric: no authority-issued clinical cutoffs; severity ladders circulating online (e.g. >3 mild, >9 severe) were NOT verifiable from allowed sources this session and must not be used. Explicit 'not a diagnostic test' disclaimer required.

calculators.name: Albumin/Globulin (A/G) Ratio Calculator
calculators.whyRelevant: Auto-explains a CMP line item using inputs (total protein, albumin) the platform already collects; low build cost.
calculators.logic: globulin = totalProtein - albumin; AG = albumin / globulin. Reference values (Cleveland Clinic Globulin Blood Test): globulin normal "2.0 to 3.5 g/dL"; "A normal A/G ratio is slightly more than 1"; "Typically, your body has slightly more albumin than globulins." Guard: albumin < totalProtein required (else entry error).
calculators.outputScale: ratio, typically 0.5-2.5

resultCategories.label: Albumin exceeds globulin (expected pattern)
resultCategories.interpretation: Matches Cleveland Clinic's description that a normal A/G ratio is slightly more than 1.
resultCategories.recommendation: No action needed based on this ratio alone; look at the individual albumin and globulin values.

resultCategories.label: Albumin does not exceed globulin
resultCategories.interpretation: Differs from the typical pattern; can occur with low albumin or elevated globulins from many causes.
resultCategories.recommendation: Nonspecific — review the underlying albumin, globulin, and total protein results with your provider.

calculators.name: Anion Gap Calculator
calculators.whyRelevant: Natural extension of the new electrolyte set; however it is primarily an acute-care/clinician tool, so consumer framing must stay purely educational — tier 3.
calculators.logic: StatPearls (NBK539757) verbatim formula: "(Na+ + K+) – (Cl- + HCO3-) = Anion Gap"; commonly used without K+ as (Na+) – (Cl- + HCO3-). Normal range (StatPearls): "4 to 12 mmol/L". Albumin correction (StatPearls): "Every 1 g/L decrease in albumin will decrease the anion gap by 0.25 mmol/L" (equivalently "every decrease of 10 g/L albumin = a 2.3 mmol/L decrease in the anion gap") — corrected gap = gap + 0.25 x (40 - albumin_g/L) when albumin is provided.
calculators.outputScale: mmol/L, typically 0-30

resultCategories.label: Within StatPearls normal range (without-K formula)
resultCategories.interpretation: Within the quoted normal range. Note the normal range depends on which formula and analyzer the lab uses.
resultCategories.recommendation: No action needed based on this value alone.

resultCategories.label: Outside normal range
resultCategories.interpretation: Anion gap abnormalities relate to acid-base status and are meaningful mainly in acute clinical contexts; low albumin lowers the apparent gap.
resultCategories.recommendation: This is a clinician-interpretation value — share with your provider rather than drawing conclusions; results from routine wellness panels are rarely actionable in isolation.

sources.title: Anion Gap

calculators.platformMapping: derived parameters with optional-input handling (ternary: include K only if provided; apply albumin correction only if provided — maps to imputation rules + ternary); bands. No missing primitives.
calculators.realWorldPresence: MDCalc 'Anion Gap'; standard in every chemistry-panel interpretation reference.
calculators.cautions: Clinical-leaning: normal range varies by formula (with-K formulas run ~4 higher) and analyzer; consumer copy must avoid acid-base diagnostic language. Consider gating behind an 'advanced' section.

calculators.name: Indirect Bilirubin Calculator
calculators.whyRelevant: Trivial companion to the new direct-bilirubin measurement so users can decompose their liver panel; limited standalone value.
calculators.logic: indirect = totalBilirubin - directBilirubin (Cleveland Clinic verbatim: unconjugated bilirubin "can't be measured directly. It's measured by subtracting the value of conjugated bilirubin from the value of total bilirubin in your blood."). Guard: direct ≤ total. Context ranges: MedlinePlus direct "less than 0.3 mg/dL", total "0.1 to 1.2 mg/dL"; Cleveland Clinic total "0.2 and 1.3 mg/dL". No verified standalone indirect band — interpret via total and direct bands only.
calculators.outputScale: mg/dL

resultCategories.label: Total and direct within reference
resultCategories.interpretation: Both measured fractions are within their reference ranges; the derived indirect value is correspondingly unremarkable.
resultCategories.recommendation: No action needed based on these values alone.

resultCategories.label: One or both fractions out of range
resultCategories.range: total > 1.2 mg/dL or direct ≥ 0.3 mg/dL (MedlinePlus thresholds)
resultCategories.interpretation: Whether the elevation is mostly direct or indirect points to different causes (e.g. benign Gilbert syndrome is a common cause of isolated indirect elevation) — this distinction is for a clinician to make.
resultCategories.recommendation: Share the full liver panel with your provider; isolated mild indirect elevation is often benign but should be confirmed.
